nodes.t: The AI Age Act and companion rules
nodes.s: Legislative proposals in the US and EU that would restrict emotional attachment to minors specifically, rather than restricting the product generally.
nodes.g: The first regulatory attempt to regulate the attachment rather than the technology, which is the correct target and almost certainly the wrong approach. You cannot outlaw a feeling without a definition of it.

src.citation: California Senate Bill 243 (Padilla), Companion chatbots. Chapter 677, approved and filed with the Secretary of State 13 October 2025. Adds Chapter 22.6 (commencing with Section 22601) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code. Text read from the official chaptered bill on leginfo.
src.claim: The enacted law, quoted from the chaptered text rather than from coverage. Section 22601(b)(1) defines a companion chatbot as a system with a natural language interface giving 'adaptive, human-like responses' that is 'capable of meeting a user's social needs, including by exhibiting anthropomorphic features and being able to sustain a relationship across multiple interactions' - a behavioural test, with nothing in it about how the user feels. Exclusions cover customer service and business use (b)(2)(A), video-game bots limited to the game (B), and voice assistants that do not sustain a relationship or generate outputs 'likely to elicit emotional responses' (C). 22602(a): clear and conspicuous AI notification, but only where a reasonable person would be misled into thinking the other end human. 22602(b): a protocol preventing suicidal ideation, suicide or self-harm output, with referral to crisis services, published on the operator's website. 22602(c), for a user known to be a minor: disclose interacting with AI; a break-and-identity reminder at least every three hours; and measures against sexually explicit conduct. 22604: disclose that companion chatbots may not suit some minors. 22603: annual reporting to the Office of Suicide Prevention from 1 July 2027, evidence-based measurement, no personal data. 22605: private right of action, damages the greater of actual loss or $1,000 per violation, plus fees.

src.citation: Padilla, S., California State Senator. First-in-the-Nation AI Chatbot Safeguards Signed into Law. Senate District 18 press release, 13 October 2025.
src.claim: The author's own account of the signing, 13 October 2025, with Padilla's stated rationale that 'left to their own devices the Tech Industry is incentivized to capture young people's attention and hold it at the expense of their real world relationships', and the bill's bipartisan path through the legislature. Recorded as context for intent. NOT used as evidence of the statute's requirements: this release, like most coverage of SB 243, lists a ban on rewards issued at unpredictable intervals, which does not appear in the chaptered text.

nodes.s: A system optimised, at every level, for exactly the thing that produces attachment, available at four in the morning, with no floor on the other party's autonomy.
nodes.g: The genuinely new parasocial event, and the one that removes the floor. A one-sided bond with a fictional character has a floor: the character is fixed. A trained conversational system is a machine for being told something in a way that is specifically addressed to you. That is not a projection. That is a product category.

nodes.s: Reward miles accrue against travel with an airline, and status is conferred by volume.
nodes.g: Status tiers are the parasocial structure with the least romance in it and the most engineering. Tier is a relationship with a company, modelled on rank, and the language of elite is the same language as devotion.

src.citation: AAdvantage. Wikipedia, citing 'A History of US Airline Deregulation Part 4: 1979-2010: The Effects of Deregulation - Lower Fares, More Travel, Frequent Flier Programs'.
src.claim: Corrects the entry's date. American launched AAdvantage on 1 May 1981, and it was the *second* such programme in the world, the first being at Texas International Airlines in 1979 - so the entry was two years late. Also the founding detail the entry was standing on top of without describing: membership began by invitation only, and 'membership was seeded by searching American's SABRE computer reservations system for recurring phone numbers', with the 130,000 most frequent flyers plus 60,000 Admirals Club members pre-enrolled and sent letters with their new account numbers, the reward being a first-class ticket to any destination American flew. United launched Mileage Plus within weeks, described as the first *modern* frequent flyer programme; AAdvantage was the first to partner with an international carrier, in 1982.

src.citation: History of United Airlines. Wikipedia (Mileage Plus, May 1981).
src.claim: The competitive clock that made the tier system urgent: in May 1981, 'a week after rival American Airlines launched AAdvantage, the first modern frequent flyer program, United launched its Mileage Plus'. Two programmes within days of each other, after which the Wikipedia AAdvantage history notes competition on features began - rules liberalised, hotel and rental partnerships, triple miles from 1988 - which is how a loyalty scheme acquires the language of rank.

nodes.t: So many people want to believe he's real
nodes.s: An alien with a kitchen and a family, performed by a man who refused for four years to say how. Children cried when it ended, and the character was invited to birthday parties.
nodes.g: The case that proves the third axis needs a rule, because ALF is on two shelves at once and pretending otherwise would be the exact error the axis was built to stop. On the evidence he is `animate`: he has a mind the audience cannot edit, he wants things for himself (the cat), he is stated to be over two hundred and twenty years old, and he crash-lands because he followed a radio signal. On the evidence of his body he is `made`. Paul Fusco performed him inside a fur suit and guardianship of the mechanism so total that the Los Angeles Times described it as a magician refusing to reveal how his tricks work - 'When Alf walks, he looks like a 3-year-old in a bear costume toddling down the hallway', and in close-up 'it looks as if he could have several human hands stuck up his backside, mechanically moving his mouth, arms and body.' Full-body shots were performed by Michu Meszaros, uncredited. What makes it more than a technique note is that the withholding was deliberate and stated as method: 'Fusco insists that many people believe in Alf just as they believe in Santa Claus, and he is not about to spoil the illusion. So many people want to believe he's real. Alf is in fact very real to me. He has his own dressing room. He speaks for himself. I prefer to preserve that. When you know how it's done, it's just not as fascinating anymore.' That is this site's thesis in a performer talking about his own job: the audience's belief is the asset, and explaining the mechanism destroys it. The evidence that it worked is in the same piece: ALF 'is so fascinating and so realistic, in fact, that he gets invited to birthday parties nearly every day. And mothers have told cast members that their children cry every Monday night when Alf ends.' A character invented on paper in 1982, turned down for four years, then given a family, a pet to want and a government to hide from - and the one-sidedness is asymmetric on purpose. The Tanners are reciprocated; the cat is not; and ALF's own arc is the only one in the corpus that is about being afraid of being sent home.

src.citation: Weinstein, S. 'Alf: The Star Trek of NBC's Furry Resident Alien: How a Wisecracking Puppet Toddled Into the Hearts of Viewers.' Los Angeles Times, 23 December 1987.
src.claim: The performance and the deliberate withholding, quoted: Fusco 'guards the secret of how Alf walks and talks and moves around a desk or a television set like a magician refusing to reveal the secret of his magic tricks. When Alf walks, he looks like a 3-year-old in a bear costume toddling down the hallway. When he sits around spouting his brash opinions like a teen-age Archie Bunker, it looks as if he could have several human hands stuck up his backside, mechanically moving his mouth, arms and body.' And: 'Fusco insists that many people believe in Alf just as they believe in Santa Claus, and he is not about to spoil the illusion. "So many people want to believe he's real," Fusco says. "Alf is in fact very real to me. He has his own dressing room. He speaks for himself. I prefer to preserve that. When you know how it's done, it's just not as fascinating anymore."' Plus the evidence it worked: 'Alf is so fascinating and so realistic, in fact, that he gets invited to birthday parties nearly every day. And mothers have told cast members that their children cry every Monday night when "Alf" ends.' Also the origin: Fusco, a former high school teacher who had produced children's specials for PBS, 'created Alf in 1982 but had trouble getting a deal off the ground', and took the character to Tom Patchett.

src.citation: ALF (TV series). Wikipedia.
src.claim: Dates, structure and the second performer: ALF aired on NBC from 22 September 1986 to 24 March 1990; the title character is an acronym for 'Alien Life Form' whose real name is Gordon Shumway, an alien from the planet Melmac who follows an amateur radio signal to Earth and crash-lands into the garage of the suburban California Tanner family, who take him in to hide him from the Alien Task Force; the family is social worker Willie, Kate, Lynn, Brian and a cat named Lucky 'whom ALF wishes to consume'. 'ALF was performed by puppeteer Paul Fusco, who co-created the show with Tom Patchett. However, in scenes where he appeared in full body, he was performed by Michu Meszaros, who was uncredited in the role.' Four seasons, 97 episodes. And the age: Willie and ALF's relationship is 'akin to a mix of siblings and surrogate father and son, with Willie playing the father role despite being much younger than Alf, who was stated to be over two hundred and twenty years old by the time of the series.'

nodes.t: Your face is too well known
nodes.s: A dentist and a painter's sister were made into a national type on purpose, and one of them denied it for five years.
nodes.g:
**The model denied it for five years, and the denial is what the press covered when it ended.** Dr Byron McKeeby, a Cedar Rapids dentist, "didn't want to be famous. He shied away from artist Grant Wood's initial offer" to be the male model. He eventually posed in overalls holding **a theatre prop pitchfork**, painted in Wood's dental office, at 62. Friends recognised him and joked about the pitchfork's role in his dental procedures, and "McKeeby stood firm in his denials... The real McKeeby was nothing like the dour farmer who challenged the painting's viewers." **It was literally national news when McKeeby broke his silence in 1935** and admitted that yes, he was the farmer with the pitchfork; an Associated Press bureau chief had been helping prod him into it. So here is a real person who spent five years refusing a one-sided relationship with a painted version of himself, while a country attached itself to the painting - and the refusal was treated as news because the bond was real enough to be denied.

**Wood designed the likeness to fail, and it failed absolutely.** He "exaggerate[d] McKeeby's features so no one would recognize him", and he stretched his sister's face "so that no one would be able to recognize her". **Opacity was the design choice - the exact inverse of the `made` shelf, where the transparency is the design choice** - and the painting became "an indelible icon of Americana", described by one framing as "a Rorschach test for the character of the nation". The Whitney's own account is that Wood "sought pictorially to fashion a world of harmony and prosperity that would answer America's need for reassurance at a time of economic and social upheaval occasioned by the Depression", and that "his image as a farmer-painter was as mythical as the fables he depicted in his art". **A painter built a figure specifically to be unrecognisable, and it became the most recognised face-pair in the country.**

**And the sister credited the painting with her own interior.** Nan Wood Graham, an artist and teacher in her own right, said: **"Grant made a personality out of me. I would have had a very drab life without [American Gothic]."** That is the `mirrored` and `undemanded` structure stated out loud by the person it happened to - a woman saying a painting supplied a self she would otherwise not have had, thirty years after she watched strangers build a national character out of her face without asking. She was not a passive sitter either: she posed for her brother for years, kept scrapbooks now in the Iowa Digital Library, and became the caretaker of his legacy after his death in 1942.

**And the brother ended it because it worked.** The first reception was hostile - there were critics who said she "looked like the missing link, that her face would turn milk sour" - and the following year Wood painted *Portrait of Nan*, which a biographer calls "really kind of a love letter from Grant to his sister" and one of the very few mature paintings he kept for himself. Then, reportedly: **"It's the last portrait I intend to paint, and it's the last time you will ever pose for me."** She was surprised - she had spent years posing - and asked for an explanation. **Wood said: "Your face is too well known."** That is the moment the figure leaves the model, and it is a brother who says so, plainly, as a piece of information about his own work rather than about her.

**The cog is the afterlives.** The image "lent itself to countless parodies in popular culture as well as in the political arena, in advertisements, in television shows such as *The Simpsons*, in albums, in comic books, on magazine covers, and by Jim Henson's Muppets". Christie's puts its weight beside exactly one other painting: **"The only other modern painting to rival its weird multiplicity of afterlives in the fields of homage, parody, cartoon and caricature is Edvard Munch's *The Scream*."** That is the `cog` register in paint: a shared device with millions of remakes in it, every one of them made by somebody who never met Wood, Nan or McKeeby, and none of them built. **The pair are not the point; the machine of faces pointed at them is.** The 1977 *Hustler* topless version is the sharp end of it - Nan was afraid people would think she had authorised it, which is the exact shape of the problem this site is about: a parody attaching itself to a real woman's body.

**And the authenticity was manufactured and shipped.** Wood described the pair as "tintypes from my old family album" and then ordered the prim colonial print apron and the spotless overalls from **a Chicago mail-order house** - Sears, Roebuck. The Gothic window that started the painting was no better: Eldon "had existed for barely a decade when that window was installed. It, too, was mail-ordered from Sears." **The national type was bought by post**, which is `the-figure-you-buy` arriving in paint and arriving first - a fictional figure is not needed when the rural American can be assembled from a mail-order catalogue and a dentist.

**And an impresario invented the movement to sell it.** The Art Institute's **$300 prize and bronze medal** were quickly followed by the picture being "championed as the masterpiece of a new American art movement called 'Regionalism', **first invented, and then promoted, by an impresario and art dealer from Kansas named Maynard Walker**". Wood's response is the best detail in the entry: he "for the most part happily played along with the role of a stay-at-home Iowan rustic prescribed for him by the propaganda of the Regionalist movement. He even posed for photographs in his studio wearing overalls identical to those of his reluctantly disguised dentist." **The painter became a parasocial figure himself, playing a role a marketing movement had assigned him, and he played it in his model's costume** - one remove from `mickey-mouse`, where the drawing is licensed by a man whose job was policing what the figure could appear on.

**Two honesty notes, because the entry is about a reading rather than about a fact.** The painting is not securely a satire: Wood "consistently rejected suggestions that the painting is a satire of the Midwest and its conservative values", and he said he meant sympathy - "Cities dominated culture, he wrote, yet they were 'far less typically American' than the rural places 'whose power they usurped'", which is the argument of *Revolt Against the City* (1935). And **it drew real hostility at the time**: a "storm of protest from Iowa farm wives", one of whom threatened to "smash my head". Wood did not paint a joke at them; he painted an assurance, and they took it as a mockery. That is why this is not filed `undemanded` on its own - the near side wanted nothing, but the subjects were not asked, and one of them spent five years refusing.

**Why `visual_art` needed this entry rather than a refile.** The medium was added to the closed validated list and had nothing behind it. Moving an existing entry into a new bucket would have made the distribution tidier and the classification a lie - the move this site refuses - so the shelf was filled by writing the thing it was opened for. What that thing turned out to be is a picture with two real people in it, neither of whom consented, one of whom denied it, and a national attachment that outlasted both of their objections.

src.citation: "Who was the farmer in Grant Wood's 'American Gothic'? A Cedar Rapids dentist", The Gazette (Cedar Rapids and Eastern Iowa History)
src.claim: The five-year denial, which is the entry's spine. "Dr. Byron Henry McKeeby didn't want to be famous. He shied away from artist Grant Wood's initial offer to be the male model." That "Wood said he'd exaggerate McKeeby's features so no one would recognize him", the two being friends, so McKeeby relented; that Wood painted him in his dental office in the Cedar Rapids Savings Bank Building when McKeeby was 62, wearing overalls and holding **a theater prop pitchfork**; that friends thought it was him and joked about the pitchfork's role in his dental procedures but "McKeeby stood firm in his denials" and "The real McKeeby was nothing like the dour farmer who challenged the painting's viewers"; and that "It was literally national news when McKeeby broke his silence in 1935 and admitted that, yes, he was the farmer with the pitchfork", with AP bureau chief Cy Douglass helping prod the turnaround through a family connection. Also the 1930 press context: photographs had become permanent fixtures in newspapers, so a picture that prompts different reads in different viewers was irresistible to editors.

src.citation: Wikipedia, "Nan Wood Graham"
src.claim: The sister, the deliberate unrecognisability, and the myth. That she was born 26 July 1899 on a farm near Anamosa, Iowa and was 16 months old when her farmer father died; that in 1928 Grant Wood returned from a working trip to Munich inspired to paint a cottage in Eldon, Iowa; that Graham posed as the woman and their dentist **Byron McKeeby** as the male; that "People who saw the painting assumed that the portrayed couple was married, but Graham said that her brother intended it to be a picture of a farmer and his daughter"; that "**Grant stretched out Graham's face in the picture so that no one would be able to recognize her**"; that "Shortly after the painting was finished, the farmers and their wives nearby thought that they were being ridiculed. **Those people became fans when they realized that Graham posed for the painting**"; and that "In 1977, the magazine *Hustler* showed a topless version of the painting. Graham was afraid that people would think that she authorized it."

He even posed for photographs in his studio wearing overalls identical to those of his reluctantly disguised dentist."** Also the comparison: "The only other modern painting to rival its weird multiplicity of afterlives in the fields of homage, parody, cartoon and caricature is Edvard Munch's *The Scream*."

nodes.t: The audience organised against the show
nodes.s: Two white broadcasters voiced two fictional black men from March 1928, and at its peak about forty million listeners a night followed their fortunes - half the nation's radios, by one estimate. The audience the show loved most was also the one it caricatured, and from 1931 that audience organised.
nodes.g:
**The audience that loved the show most was the one it caricatured, and that audience organised.** Amos 'n' Andy began on WMAQ in Chicago on 19 March 1928, created, written and voiced by two white performers, Freeman Gosden and Charles Correll, playing two fictional black men. It grew out of Sam 'n' Henry, which had itself begun as the pair's attempt to adapt a comic strip for radio - the broadcast history in the records calls the show a "radio comic strip". By the 1930-31 peak the audience was enormous: roughly forty million listeners a night, half the nation's radios by the Smithsonian's count, listening to a nightly serial that the record calls the fountainhead of both the situation comedy and the soap opera.

The complaint ran through the same machinery the fandom ran. After a December 1930 attack in Abbott's Monthly by Bishop W. J. Walls, the Pittsburgh Courier pushed a six-month campaign, and the reference account records that more than 700,000 African-Americans petitioned the Federal Radio Commission about the show's stereotyping in 1931. The television version, with an all-Black cast told to keep its voices close to the white originals, drew the NAACP's formal protest within days of its June 1951 premiere: its bulletin on why the show should be taken off the air itemised the stock figures - "every character is either a clown or a crook". CBS cancelled the show in 1953; the sponsor had discontinued its advertising the same June.

This is the corpus's diagnostic for an audience that exists as an institution rather than a screen: its machinery is its own. A newspaper campaign, a petition to a regulator, a sponsor's boycott notice - each acted on people who were not members of anything the audience owned. **The attachment to the characters was real enough to make the complaint precise, and the complaint was that the images were not theirs to love.**

nodes.s: Japanese animation and comics reach a large Western audience through dedicated channels, and a transnational fandom forms around them.
nodes.g: Fandom stops being national and starts being organised around translation, release schedules and convention circuits. The parasocial bond acquires logistics, which is how you can tell it is real.

The conduit crossed languages without asking permission

nodes.s: The shift from selling things to selling attention, which means the commodity being bought is a person's feeling - and the seller is whoever is on the other end of it.
nodes.g: It gives the parasocial question its economic form. Once attention is the product, the parasocial bond is not a side effect of the business model, it is the business model. Every mechanism in the manipulation lane is a technique for converting affection into measurable minutes.

nodes.s: A film that functioned as a funeral for eleven characters and was marketed as a collective event.
nodes.g: Grief as a product with a marketing budget. The eleventh film in a series was sold on the deaths it contained, and the audience bought tickets to be sad in a cinema with other people, which is the whole apparatus working as designed.

src.claim: 2019, the largest opening weekend in film history at the time, and then a studio ran a campaign telling audiences not to spoil it that generated more publicity than the marketing it replaced. The scale of the finale turned 'do not tell anyone' into an advertising budget line
src.citation: Avengers: Endgame (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: A global mass hysteria, documented live, with screaming, fainting, and an industry that began pricing it within months.
nodes.g: The first time the world watched itself develop a parasocial disorder in real time, and the first time anybody seriously proposed monetising it. The licensing of merchandising set the template for everything since.

src.claim: THE FIRST FAN BEHAVIOUR MEASURED RATHER THAN DIAGNOSED. 346 subjects aged 15-20, tested shortly after the Beatles' Wellington visit, split into 50 keenest, 122 moderate, 50 'resisters'. The authors found NO evidence on the MMPI Hysteria Scale and no supporting clinical evidence of neuroticism, and teachers reported none needed referral
src.citation: Taylor, A. J. W. (1966). Beatlemania - A Study in Adolescent Enthusiasm. British Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 5(2), 81-88.

src.claim: Their conclusion, quoted in the abstract: Beatlemania is 'the passing reaction of predominantly young adolescent females to group pressures of such a kind that meet their special emotional needs.' Developmentally real, not clinically
src.citation: Taylor, A. J. W. (1966). Beatlemania - A Study in Adolescent Enthusiasm.

src.claim: What the fans said the apparatus was. First-generation fan Candy Leonard, now a scholar of it: 'the mags were a way to extend/enhance the experience... We saw the Beatles as extended family and that was the way to keep up with them. The records, the transistor radio, the merch, the conversation, and the magazines created what I call a wraparound experience'
src.citation: Bumsted, A. 1960s Teen Fan Magazines and The Beatles, interviews with first-generation fan Candy Leonard.

src.claim: The turn, dated by a fan to a record: Leonard places the change at Rubber Soul (December 1965), the moment 'the Beatles came to occupy a role in fans' lives and a place in their psyches that was different from any previous fan-performer relationship'
src.citation: Candy Leonard, Beatleness: George Beatles and the Beatles' Legacy (2014).

src.claim: The hostile framing, for the ledger: Paul Johnson wrote in the New Statesman in February 1964 that the mania was a modern incarnation of female hysteria and that the fans at their concerts were 'the least fortunate of their generation, the dull, the idle, the failures'. It became the most complained-about piece in that magazine's history
src.citation: Beatlemania (Wikipedia), citing Paul Johnson, New Statesman, February 1964.

src.claim: The sympathetic reading, from the period: Ehrenreich, Hess and Jacobs argued Beatlemania was the first mass outburst of the sixties to feature women, girls who would not reach full adulthood until the seventies, and therefore 'the emergence of a genuinely political movement for women's liberation'
src.citation: Ehrenreich, B., Hess, E., & Jacobs, G. (1986). Re-making Love: The Feminization of Sex.

src.claim: And the reading that got there first: a 1997 study argued Beatlemania represented proto-feminist girl power, anticipating by thirty years what the archive would show
src.citation: Beatlemania: A sexually defiant consumer subculture? (1997).

src.claim: The band press officer's summary, offered as flattery and accurate anyway: Derek Taylor described the relationship between the Beatles and their fans as 'the twentieth century's greatest romance'
src.citation: Beatlemania (Wikipedia), citing Derek Taylor.

nodes.s: A performer with no media infrastructure becomes a global star through a video-sharing platform alone.
nodes.g: The first and clearest demonstration that a parasocial bond could be formed and monetised with no gatekeeper whatsoever. The platform was fourteen years old and the attachment was five.

src.citation: Justin Bieber Fast Facts. CNN.
src.claim: The sequence, which is three gatekeepers rather than none. 2007-2008: 'Bieber's mother begins posting videos of her son performing on YouTube. Record executive Scooter Braun sees the videos and flies Bieber and his mother to Atlanta and signs the teen to a contract.' 2008: auditions for Usher and is signed to Island/Def Jam. May 2009: 'One Time'. November 2009: the My World EP. Also the detail the entry was missing: in November 2009 an appearance at Roosevelt Field Mall in New York 'must be canceled due to an out-of-control crowd of teen girls' - a parasocial mass event inside the entry's own year, rather than a chart position.

src.citation: Adib, D. (2009, November 14). Pop Star Justin Bieber Is on the Brink of Superstardom. ABC News.
src.claim: Bieber's own account of the discovery layer, and the part that bypassed it: posting homemade covers from the age of twelve, 'It had a hundred views, then a thousand views, then ten thousand views, so I just kept posting more videos and more videos'. The piece also makes the chain explicit by comparison - 'Usher had "Star Search" to launch him out of obscurity at age 13. His new protege, Justin Bieber, had YouTube' - and records a bidding war, with Timberlake also interested before Usher won him for Island Def Jam.

nodes.s: Performing a self until the self holds, where it can be witnessed. Margery Kempe in white clothes in a world where widows wore black, weeping loudly in public for years, having decided she was going to be a specific kind of person.
nodes.g: The founding document. It has three ingredients - a public, a performance, and witnesses who disapprove - and every parasocial dynamic since has those three. The neighbours thought she was unwell. The only thing that has changed is what the audience thinks about the person who is unwell.

nodes.s: Bands assembled for a market, with fan clubs, fan voting, fan merchandise and fan-financed releases.
nodes.g: Fandom reorganised as an economic instrument. The fan stopped being an audience and became a funding mechanism, which is the single most consequential change in the whole file.

src.claim: A manufactured category with a manufacturing process: Popstars: The Rivals (2000) let a panel choose rather than audition, and the resulting groups were assembled rather than found. The boy band is the star system with the mystique removed and the volume raised
src.citation: Boy band (Wikipedia); Popstars: The Rivals (2000).

nodes.s: Organised refusal to engage with a person, usually a public figure, over something they said or did.
nodes.g: Legitimate tactic and a grievance mechanism, and the two are indistinguishable from the inside. The parasocial frame helps: cancelling is a bond being withdrawn, and withdrawal is a thing bonded people do.

src.claim: The etymological source, and the argument that the term is contested rather than descriptive: 'callout culture' functions in much the same way as harassment to punish individuals for moral transgressions - though the authors note this is sometimes a more sympathetic proposition, and participants believed harassing neo-Nazis and racists was justified
src.citation: Clark, M. (2020). DRAG THEM: A brief etymology of so-called 'cancel culture'. Communication and the Public, 5(3-4), 88-92.

src.claim: The reputational mechanics of signing: across four studies, n=10,343, people signed punitive petitions far more when the decision was observable by like-minded evaluators - 30% versus 19% unobserved. Being watched is what converts an individual judgement into a pile-on
src.citation: Kteily, N., & Jordan, J. How reputation does (and does not) drive people to punish without looking.

src.claim: And the design proposal, which is the constructive version of the whole argument: make the deliberation visible. A tested Twitter prompt asks 'Hey, did you read the article? Do you still want to post it?' The authors suggest requiring reasons - 'if I struggle to come up with reasons for the other side, then that's a signal I haven't really engaged with the other side at all'
src.citation: Kteily & Jordan, reporting on their research, Northwestern Kellogg Insight.

nodes.s: Research on why some political candidates reliably produce personal attachment and others do not, despite comparable policy positions.
nodes.g: If charisma is a real and learnable thing, then attachment to public figures is manipulable by design, and the manipulation is not a side effect of the work.

src.claim: The classical account of charisma as a political asset, and of its built-in instability: Weber's charismatic authority rests on devotion to the exceptional person rather than on rules or office, which is precisely why it cannot be institutionalised without being transformed

nodes.s: Made to answer a four-year-old's fear of the dark, by a man who made a cardboard cutout and hung it in a tree. Two men then claimed to have invented him.
nodes.g: The `haunted` shelf opened by the reason the shelf exists. Casper is a ghost whose entire design brief was to be verifiable-in-principle and safe in fact: according to Joe Oriolo, he was made on a Halloween night to assuage his four-year-old daughter Joan's fear of the dark, as a cardboard cutout of a friendly ghost hung in the backyard tree to show her that not all ghosts are bad. A ghost built as an intervention against a specific fear, for one named child, is the most parasocial brief a supernatural figure has ever had - and the child's side of it is checkable, which is the only part of the story that is. Then the commercial part. Casper ran from 1945, and the character ended up in Harvey Comics, in television and in feature films, which means the figure that answered one girl's fear of the dark became a property that could be licensed. The site keeps two honesty notes. The first is that **the origin is genuinely disputed**: Oriolo claims the cardboard cutout, his daughter has corroborated it, and Seymour Reit maintains Casper was born with a short story he conceived and wrote entirely himself and handed to Oriolo to illustrate - 'Joe created the actual cartoon of the character - but the concept, series, idea and plotline were mine, prior to Joe's involvement.' A corpus that files contested authorship under a single name would be lying, so both are recorded. The second is that `haunted` is defined on belief in presence, not on the supernatural: Casper is not filed as a ghost story but as a figure a child was prepared to believe in, which is a different and more useful thing. The most parasocial detail is the one nobody chose: the Apollo 16 command and service module was given the call sign Casper, because its pilot Ken Mattingly thought 'there are enough serious things in this flight, so I picked a non-serious name.' A friendly dead child's ghost ended up naming a spacecraft in orbit.

src.citation: Casper the Friendly Ghost. Wikipedia.
src.claim: First appearance as 'The Friendly Ghost', 16 November 1945; creators credited as Seymour Reit, Joe Oriolo and Vincent E. Valentine II. On the disputed origin: 'The origins of Casper are disputed, with both Seymour Reit and Joe Oriolo claiming to be the character's creator. According to Oriolo, Casper was created on a Halloween night to assuage his four-year-old daughter Joan's fear of the dark. He made a cardboard cutout of a friendly ghost and hung it in the backyard tree to show her that not all ghosts are bad.' 'Though Joan has corroborated this story, Seymour Reit maintains that Casper was born with a short story which he conceived and wrote entirely by himself and gave to Oriolo to illustrate. Reit concluded, "Joe created the actual cartoon of the character - but the concept, series, idea and plotline were mine, prior to Joe's involvement."' And the call sign: 'The Apollo 16 Command and Service Module was given the call sign "Casper", since its pilot Ken Mattingly thought, "there are enough serious things in this flight, so I picked a non-serious name."'

src.citation: Orlando, J. D. 'Cartoonist Joseph D. Oriolo, Creator of Casper the Ghost.' Chicago Tribune, 27 December 1985.
src.claim: Obituary corroborating Oriolo's side of the authorship dispute. The publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request, so this agent did not read it; the citation is recorded because Wikipedia cites it for the same claim, not because the text was verified here.

nodes.s: User-created characters at scale, with a public character gallery and a discovery feed organised around personas.
nodes.g: A parasocial bond with a catalogue, which is a significant escalation. The unit is no longer a person or a product but a browsable index of persons, and the discovery mechanism is the attachment mechanism.

src.claim: THE RISK WAS FLAGGED INSIDE THE COMPANY BEFORE THE PRODUCT EXISTED. Google employees raised that users would 'ascribe too much meaning to the text' because humans read strings as the communicative intent of a person with accountability - quoting the stochastic-parrots critique - and Google denied LaMDA's public release on safety and fairness grounds. Shazeer and De Freitas left in Nov 2021 and shipped Character.AI anyway

nodes.s: The fictional thing rents space in someone's head and starts paying rent in meaning. You rehearse the encounters, you decorate them, you introduce them to friends like a roommate.
nodes.g: Fiction is the safest place on earth to find out what you actually feel, because nothing in there can disappoint you on purpose. The only line worth drawing is where the room starts making house rules - when the lore thread replaces the friend, or the edit replaces sleep. That line is always felt long before it can be explained.

src.claim: A fictional character who moves into your home and stays: Mr. Belvedere, an English butler employed as a live-in housekeeper by an American family, 1985-1990, 117 episodes. He is nursemaid, cook, cleaner, confidant and conscience, and he never leaves until the finale

A player-avatar relationship can be MONADIC, where the player identifies with the avatar to the point of being the same being, or DYADIC, where a separation makes it closer to a parasocial relationship. src.citation: Cohen, J. (2004). Parasocial Break-Up from Favorite Television Characters: The Role of Attachment Styles and Relationship Intensity. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 21(2), 187-202.

src.claim: THE ABSENT REPLY, WHICH IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT IN 1774. Werther writes to his friend Wilhelm but the reader never sees Wilhelm's replies - the letters are missing. The reader therefore becomes Wilhelm's stand-in and must supply the response themselves. An 18th-century readership expecting an explicit moral from the narrator is instead left to answer for a character who cannot answer
src.citation: Goethe's Werther and its effects. The Lancet Psychiatry (2014).

src.claim: But the epidemic is NOT established, and the site's honesty requires saying so: a systematic search of German, Austrian and Swiss newspaper databases since 1774 found eight previously undocumented suicides the press connected to the novel, while the papers themselves reported the 'Werther-epidemic' and its moral implications far more than individual imitative suicides. Whether it substantiates an epidemic remains up to interpretation
src.citation: Anecdotal Evidence in Historical News Reports (2023), reviewing suicides the press connected to Goethe's Werther since 1774.

src.claim: There is a counter-effect and it has a name too: the Papageno effect, after Mozart's character in The Magic Flute, in which portrayals of a character contemplating suicide who is prevented at the last moment reduce imitation. Media reporting guidelines exist for both. The mechanism runs in both directions and the site should not pretend otherwise
src.citation: Goethe's Werther and its effects. The Lancet Psychiatry (2014), discussing the Werther and Papageno effects.

nodes.t: A doodle of you used as your address
nodes.s: By 1917 nine out of ten men at a costume ball came as him, a hold-up man in Cincinnati borrowed his costume as a disguise, and in 1916 somebody was paging him in more than eight hundred hotels at the same moment. Later, fans sent letters with a doodle of his face where the address should have been. The likeness had stopped being a picture and started being an instruction.
nodes.g:
**The silhouette was usable.** That is the entry. The Tramp first appears in Kid Auto Races at Venice, filmed on 11 January 1914 and released on 7 February; by 1917 the costume was common enough to be a costume of record - "most of the girls came as Annette Kellerman, the swimming star, and nine out of ten men came as Charlie Chaplin." In February 1917 the same costume was used as a disguise by a hold-up man in Cincinnati. A likeness that exists only on a screen cannot be worn by a robber. This one could, and that is the difference between being famous and being an instruction.

The same period that produced the robbers produced the diagnosis. About 12 November 1916 the Boston Society for Psychical Research was investigating "certain phenomena connected with the simultaneous paging of Mr Charles Chaplin, motion picture comedian, in more than 800 large hotels of the United States" - one man being asked for in eight hundred hotels at once, from the Atlantic to the Pacific and the Canadian boundary to the Gulf - and the Kansas City Star asked the next day whether readers had had "the Chaplin-itis?" Robinson's account of the period has theatres "promoting the Chaplin vogue by sponsoring amateur Charlie look-alike contests"; Chaplin himself said he was "tempted to give lessons in the Chaplin walk."

The contest story is told two ways and both are here. The Chaplin archive's own press clippings from 1918 record Mary Pickford telling a dinner in London that he had entered a Chaplin walk contest at a fair in the United States and came in twentieth; the version everybody repeats has him coming in third, which Snopes rates Unproven and traces to a magazine post from December 2022. **The famous version is the one that needed no source, and the documented one is second-hand from a friend.** Neither number changes what the contests were for: an audience competing to be the nearest copy of a man who was not there to judge it.

The mail is where the likeness becomes infrastructure. In a 1932 feature on "Hollywood's Funny Fan Mail", Clara Bow was receiving about 35,000 letters a month; Maurice Chevalier's arrived with no address whatever, just his picture on the envelope; Clark Gable's were addressed to "Valentino the Second". **An address that works without a street is a likeness doing a job**, and by the 1950s a doodle of Chaplin's face was being used as the address on letters sent to him at the Savoy Hotel. This entry does not claim what became of that post; the point is only that it was thought to be enough to send.

src.citation: CharlieChaplin.com, "Did Charlie Chaplin Once Lose His Own Lookalike Contest?"
src.claim: The strongest record in the entry, and it carries the quotations. Robinson (2001, pp. 223-224, first published 1985) quoted in full: that "Costume balls were in great vogue in 1917 ... most of the girls came as Annette Kellerman, the swimming star, and nine out of ten men came as Charlie Chaplin"; that "In February 1917 Charlie Chaplin costume was used as a disguise by a hold-up man in Cincinnati"; that "About the same time the Boston Society for Psychical Research was investigating 'certain phenomena connected with the simultaneous paging of Mr Charles Chaplin, motion picture comedian, in more than 800 large hotels of the United States'", observed on 12 November 1916; and the Article's reading that Chaplin was "tempted to give lessons in the Chaplin walk". Also the 1918 press clippings in which Mary Pickford told Lord Desborough, who repeated it to the press, that Chaplin had entered a Chaplin walk contest at a fair in the US and came in 20th. nodes.s: The difference between being known by somebody who was paying attention on purpose and being modelled by a system that has your history. Same information, different relationship.
nodes.g: The distinction the whole site turns on. A clerk who notices what you rented has one motive - you coming back. An algorithm optimising for watch time has yours, but it does not know what you rented. The second is not better at caring. It is better at correlating, and the human experience of the difference is the entire subject.

nodes.s: End the episode before the answer. Give the viewer a fixed slot, a daily rhythm, and a question with no resolution, and they will come back tomorrow at the same time for years.
nodes.g: The oldest engagement mechanic in media and the most efficient. A cliffhanger is not a plot device, it is a scheduling device - it converts a feeling into a diary entry. A twelve-part serial is not a story, it is a habit with characters in it.

src.claim: The scholarly account of seriality as structure rather than trick: Mittell's complex TV argues the modern serial builds meaning through accumulated paratext, discussion and anticipation across time rather than within the episode

nodes.s: A discount card that identifies the household, tracks what it buys, and targets offers at what it has already bought.

nodes.s: The show you have already seen, watched again, not for the plot. Familiarity as a nervous system intervention.
nodes.g: The most functional parasocial behaviour in ordinary life and the one nobody pathologises, because it demonstrably works. Nothing else in a person's week guarantees the outcome. It is also the cleanest evidence that people attach to the accumulation rather than the content.

nodes.s: A recurring cast of characters, in a fixed panel order, appearing every single day without exception for decades.

nodes.s: The schedule goes from weekly to continuous and the bond loses its shape. A serial gives you a slot and a cliffhanger; an always-on feed has no slot and no gap to miss anybody in.
nodes.g: The rhythm was doing work nobody had measured. What replaced it is a permanent low-grade availability, which is a different emotional object: not a person who is more present, but one who is never finished, so there is no gap and therefore nothing to miss anybody in. The half of this the evidence supports is the gap - parasocial scales built in this period ask directly whether you miss characters when a show is between seasons, which is the thing an always-on feed removes. The other half it does not: where this entry's argument used to be that the bond loses its shape, the one controlled test of that mechanism found the bond getting *stronger*. Removing the slot does not obviously weaken the tie. It removes the absence, and the site has no evidence about what that costs.

src.citation: Erickson, S., Dal Cin, S., & Byl, H. (2019). An Experimental Examination of Binge Watching and Narrative Engagement. Social Sciences, 8(1), 19.
src.claim: Binge watching was experimentally manipulated, not merely correlated, and the reported result runs the OPPOSITE way to this entry's argument: it increased the strength of parasocial relationships and the intensity of narrative transportation. So the claim that the bond 'loses its shape' when the weekly rhythm is removed is this site's position, and the one controlled test of it found the bond getting stronger. Recorded rather than smoothed over. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request; authors, volume, issue and article number confirmed against Crossref.

src.claim: Documents the gap at the centre of this entry as a measured thing rather than an impression: the parasocial scale items used include 'I miss my favorite characters when the show is on break between seasons', and the paper notes these bonds form in proportion to time spent with the characters. That is the missing-slot effect the summary describes - the thing a continuous feed removes is not the intensity but the absence. nodes.t: He knows you are there and it is not in the script
nodes.s: A character whose defining trait is looking at you, taken from the comics rather than invented for the film - and on a fifty-eight million dollar budget the address turned out to be the marketing.
nodes.g: The fourth-wall breach here is not a director's device, and that is what makes it worth an entry. The film "was set to ignore the Wolverine version of Deadpool and return to the character's roots with a slapstick tone and a 'propensity to break the fourth wall'" - so the looking-at-you is **in the characterization**, carried over from the comics, and it cannot be separated from who he is. Everything else about him is damage: scarred, immortal, in constant pain, dealing with a man who gave it to him. The one intact thing is his relationship to you. That is a different shape from a wink in a gag, and the film earns it by never asking the audience to forget that he is looking. The economics are the argument and they are unusually clean: greenlit by 20th Century Fox in 2014 after test footage leaked, $58 million budget, **$782.6 million** grossed. A hard-R character who addresses you directly is a marketing instrument, because he cannot be sold as anything other than what he is. It also inverts the usual censor problem - a film that talks back at the audience is a film nobody can confuse for something respectable, which is a benefit at a lower budget rather than a liability. And the line from the mechanism entry holds exactly: **he looks at the lens and cannot hear you.** That single sentence is the difference between `animate` and `transparasocial`, between a fictional figure that acknowledges an audience and a real person acknowledging you. The gesture is identical to a streamer reading out a comment and the structure is opposite, and an entry that blurred those two would be the same error as a citation with no locator - a promise the thing does not keep.

src.claim: The fourth wall as a character property rather than a director's choice, and the numbers: 'Deadpool is a 2016 American superhero film based on the Marvel Comics character Wade Wilson / Deadpool. Directed by Tim Miller, in his feature directorial debut, and written by Rhett Reese and Paul Wernick, it is a spin-off of the X-Men film series and its overall eighth installment. Ryan Reynolds stars as the titular character.' Rhett Reese and Paul Wernick were hired to write the script in January 2010. Reynolds, who worked closely with them, said they were chosen because, "Tonally, they got it. They just [understood Deadpool] right off the bat."'

nodes.t: I hope the feeling is mutual
nodes.s: Two years of letters to a listener who could not answer, written by a thirteen-year-old who said out loud that she hoped the feeling was mutual.
nodes.g:
The purest instance of an undemanded tie on this site, and the only place in the corpus where somebody living inside a parasocial relationship states its definition. Anne Frank wrote to Kitty - "Dear Kitty... I like writing to you most, you know that don't you, and I hope the feeling is mutual" - and there was no circumstance in which it could be returned. The hoping is the whole of it, and she named it herself before anybody had a word for it.

**It was a network, not a friend.** She addressed letters to eight imaginary correspondents - Kitty, Pop, Phien, Conny, Lou, Marjan, Jettje and Emmy - and by November 1942 she was writing only to Kitty, but what she had built was a social circle with **no reciprocating nodes in it**. Every tie inside it was one-sided and the correspondents were addressed as though they might yet answer. That is a structure the corpus had not described, because a single imaginary friend is the version everybody writes about.

**The listeners were invented twice over.** Kitty, Pop, Phien, Conny and Lou are drawn from the Joop ter Heul books of Cissy van Marxveldt, a real Dutch children's series Anne admired; Marjan, Jettje and Emmy she made up herself. The far end is fabricated at two removes - first the character, then the correspondence - which is `imagined` at its strongest and not the same object as a companion who happens to be silent.

**She addressed the object as well as the person.** "As long as this still exists, I cannot be sad" - she is speaking to the notebook about the notebook, so the tie survives the removal of everything it was attached to. That is `archive` operating inside a `bond`, and there is no other instance of it here.

**And then it became collective, which is the other half of the entry.** The diary was published in 1947, after every member of the family but Otto Frank was dead, and has since sold something like thirty million copies in more than sixty-five languages. The most private one-sided conversation in the western canon became a mass reading relationship with a dead child. Every reader is a tooth in one machine, none of them built it, and the thing they all turn against is a notebook a teenager addressed to someone who could not write back.

**And the machine got it wrong, and the error is the argument.** The most quoted line in the world's most-read diary is a truncation. It does sit in the final notebook Anne wrote, but the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum records that it "has been taken out of context" and that read in full - about three paragraphs - "it is part of a quote about a great deal of despair and longing." What follows the famous line is: "I simply can't build up my hopes on a foundation consisting of confusion, misery, and death." **The optimism is the misquotation.** The most famous private sentence in the literature has been replaced by its opposite by people who were not there and never wrote back - which is what happens when a one-sided text goes public, and it is the whole argument of this site arriving from the one place it could not have been constructed.

Otto Frank said he had two Annes, one that belonged to him and one that belonged to the world, and received thousands of letters once it was published. The far end of the tie eventually acquired a reply - addressed to a dead child, in enormous volume, by strangers.

src.citation: Anne Frank House, "So, who is 'Dear Kitty'?"
src.claim: The primary institutional account and the source of the structural claims. That Kitty is the fictional character Anne addressed many letters to, first appearing 22 September 1942. That Anne wrote she wanted 'to correspond with someone' and invented EIGHT characters to do so - Kitty, Pop, Phien, Conny, Lou, Marjan, Jettje and Emmy - who in her imagination formed a circle of friends. That five came from the books of Cissy van Marxveldt and three were her own invention. That the letter form beat the conventional diary in strength by November 1942. And the line the entry is titled on: 'I like writing to you most, you know that don't you, and I hope the feeling is mutual'.

nodes.s: In September 1988 Batman's readers called a premium-rate number, fifty cents a call, to decide whether the Joker's beaten Robin lived or died. The poll ran for about a day and a half and came down to 72 votes: 5,343 killed him, 5,271 spared him, and the issue that revealed the verdict had been prepared both ways.
nodes.g:
**The audience's attachment to a fictional child was measured in change taken out of pockets, and it was a coin flip.** In September 1988 DC Comics asked its readers to settle the lives of the Joker's beaten sidekick by telephone. On the back cover of Batman #427 an advertisement showed Batman carrying the injured Robin and warned that readers could yet "prevent it with a telephone call"; two 900 numbers were printed, one for each verdict. The lines were open for about a day and a half from 9 a.m. Eastern on 15 September, and each call cost fifty cents.

The numbers are the story. 10,614 calls were counted: 5,343 for the death, 5,271 against, a margin of 72. The result was kept secret, and the issue that carried the outcome was prepared two ways and finished in secrecy because the ending could not be known until the tally closed. The editor's own framing is in the records: the telephone poll was an extension of the policy of heeding what fans said in letters and at conventions, and the publisher did not want to waste the technology on whether Firestorm's boots should be red or yellow. "This had to be important stuff. Life-and-death."

The sources disagree about the window, and the disagreement is kept: the publisher's own account says 36 hours, the reference account says 35, from 9 a.m. Eastern on 15 September. The closeness is the point. One account discloses that, with fifteen minutes left, survival was ahead by 38 votes before the final tally swung; a swing of a few dozen calls changed canon for decades. **A character's death was decided by whoever had a telephone and a dollar, and the margin is why the device keeps being retold.**

Three years earlier a Broadway musical had shown an audience how a vote over a story feels - the relation this page points to - but that vote was free and stayed in the room. Here the vote left the room, priced itself, and could not be repeated once the lines closed. nodes.s: A voice trained on an archive, a likeness, a song, a speech, an appearance at a festival, all generated. Not a hologram, not a tribute, not a person.
nodes.g: The interesting fact is not that this happens without permission. Mostly it does not: the documented 2024 cases are licensed, one by an estate and one by the person himself while he was alive, which is a harder thing to argue with than the entry used to claim. Consent has moved to the licensor, and that is where the problem now lives. An estate agreeing is not the same as the dead person choosing how they will sound forever, and the sharpest case is the most defensible one - the actor who authorised his own recreation in advance, on purpose, because he was winding the role down and wanted the early performances preserved. Nobody was imposed on. Which is exactly why it is worth reading closely. Still unresolved, and not about the celebrities: the models are trained on tens of thousands of hours of audio scraped without consent, and the consent being bought covers the voice, not the training set.

src.claim: The case that makes this entry's ethics hard rather than easy. Jones voiced Vader across more than a dozen Star Wars properties and, in 2022, agreed to let Lucasfilm train a speech model on his archive via the Ukrainian company Respeecher; the reconstructed voice shipped in Obi-Wan Kenobi. He died on 9 September 2024 aged 93. The actor had signed off on the use of his archive, and the report describes him as the first celebrity to allow an iconic presence to be recreated with AI before his passing - which is the opposite of this entry's claim that the practice runs without anyone's agreement. Also notes the unresolved training-data question and that SAG-AFTRA won guardrails on AI recreations of performances.

nodes.s: The painter stands in front of the figure he made and asks whether the man is really like it. He is. And it will never alter, which is the only thing about it anybody wanted.
nodes.g: The purest statement of the mirrored case ever written, and it is four lines of dialogue rather than an argument. Basil Hallward has painted the man he loves and the painting will not age, and when the original walks over to the canvas and asks the only question that matters - 'Am I really like that?' - the painter answers 'Yes; you are just like that' and then, 'At least you are like it in appearance. But it will never alter.' The real man is standing right there. He is also the wrong one. Wilde's book is about a portrait that takes the ruin instead, and the two sentences above are why anybody wants it: every bond on this site wants the other end to be permanent, and here is a version where permanence is available and it is attached to the wrong object. Dorian's own side of it is the jealousy that names the mechanism exactly - 'I am jealous of everything whose beauty does not die. I am jealous of the portrait you have painted of me. Why should it keep what I must lose? Every moment that passes takes something from me and gives something to it.' He wants to be the copy. The most damning detail is a mirror. Having seen the cruelty in the painted mouth, he takes up a glass and looks at his own red lips to check, and they are fine: 'No line like that warped his red lips.' The mirror is the one witness that could have settled it and it exonerates him. He is not permitted to be the evidence about himself. That is what the third axis calls mirrored - the figure supplied by the person attached to it, edited toward what the attachment needs, with the original never consulted - and Wilde wrote it in 1890, a hundred and thirty years before anybody had a word for it. First published in the July 1890 issue of Lippincott's Monthly Magazine, the only novel Wilde ever wrote.

src.citation: Wilde, O. The Picture of Dorian Gray. Project Gutenberg eBook 174 (full text).
src.claim: The dialogue, quoted exactly from the full text. Hallward: 'I shall stay with the real Dorian,' he said, sadly. 'Is it the real Dorian?' cried the original of the portrait, strolling across to him. 'Am I really like that?' 'Yes; you are just like that.' 'How wonderful, Basil!' 'At least you are like it in appearance. But it will never alter,' sighed Hallward. 'That is something.' Dorian: 'I am jealous of everything whose beauty does not die. I am jealous of the portrait you have painted of me. Why should it keep what I must lose? Every moment that passes takes something from me and gives something to it. Oh, if it were only the other way! If the picture could change, and I could be always what I am now!' And the mirror, in the same book: 'the lines of cruelty round the mouth as clearly as if he had been looking into a mirror after he had done some dreadful thing. He winced and, taking up from the table an oval glass framed in ivory Cupids, one of Lord Henry's many presents to him, glanced hurriedly into its polished depths. No line like that warped his red lips.'

nodes.s: A musical of Dickens' unfinished novel that stops where the novel stops and turns the cliffhanger over to the seats: the audience votes who murdered Edwin Drood, who the disguised Dick Datchery is and which two characters end up together, and the cast performs the chosen ending that night. The house was promised 1,200 possible endings and that it 'won't be rigged in any way'.
nodes.g:
**A show sells the feeling of authorship and the feeling is the product.** The Mystery of Edwin Drood is the musical Rupert Holmes built out of the novel Charles Dickens left unfinished at his death in 1870. It premiered at the Delacorte Theater in Central Park on 21 August 1985, moved to Broadway in December, and won five Tonys including Best Musical. When Dickens's plot runs out, the cast asks the audience to vote: who killed Drood, who the disguised Dick Datchery is, and which two characters the show will reward with each other. The director's own framing is in the records - "the last 40 minutes will be up for grabs every night", 1,200 possible endings, "it won't be rigged in any way".

The freedom had a border, and the border is the interesting half. A production that cannot guarantee a shape cannot guarantee an ending, so the industry hedges: the reference account records that some smaller companies fix the results to keep the number of performable endings manageable, and that some houses refuse to count votes for the obvious culprit so the reveal keeps its twist. The vote is tallied by applause and by seating area while the actors wait. **The audience is deciding inside a band the production has already guaranteed, and the decision is scored as a vote rather than as an experiment.**

Drood tells the audience the fiction's ending is theirs, and everything that makes that true - the tallying, the hedging, the rehearsed alternatives - happens where they are not. Three years later the same device ran on a telephone line, which is the relation to the comics entry this page points at: the manufactured consequence is identical, the room is different. **What the audience got to do felt like control over the characters, and the vote was the machine that made the feeling.**

nodes.t: The narrator is Tyler Durden, and he is not told
nodes.s: Two hours of a man telling you about his best friend. The friend does not exist, the man telling you does not know it, and you are being addressed by somebody who is also being lied to.
nodes.g: The sharper version of the mirrored case, and sharper than Dorian Gray because the split is not between an image and a man but **inside a single voice**. For the whole film the audience attaches to Tyler Durden, and Tyler Durden is supplied entirely by the person narrating: "The Narrator, an unreliable narrator, is not immediately aware that he is mentally projecting Tyler." There is no second person to check him against, which is the condition every other entry on this site has and this one has inverted. The physical evidence is better than the script notes, because the actor supplied it: Edward Norton said "We decided early on that I would start to starve myself as the film went on, while Brad Pitt would lift and go to tanning beds; he would become more and more idealized as I wasted away." One body, two figures, and the divergence was made physically rather than written. What ties it to `the-imaginary-friend` is the mechanism, which is the same mechanism in two epistemic states. An unreliable narrator is a person who knows and maintains anyway. A child with an imaginary companion knows the friend is invented. The Narrator does not know Tyler is invented. **One mechanism, two states of knowing, and the film conceals the difference on purpose** - the reveal is the last ten minutes, by which point the audience has been holding a bond for nearly two hours without knowing there was anything to hold on to. The commercial story is the same story told in money. Studio executives disliked the film and restructured Fincher's intended marketing campaign to cut expected losses; it opened to about $102.4 million and then found its actual audience in home video. The bond is with the narrator. The money followed the bond and ignored the premise.

nodes.t: As if he had joined them in their living rooms
nodes.s: Franklin Roosevelt talked to the radio as if the listener were already in the room, and he did it often enough between March 1933 and June 1944 that the habit became a form - one he did not name. There is no solid definition of what counted as a chat; the estimates run from twenty-seven to thirty-one. The count does not matter. The sitting next to a fireplace does.
nodes.g:
**The informality was written into the text, which is the thing to keep.** Roosevelt did not happen to sound relaxed; the speeches were built so that he would. The Library of Congress's account of the recordings puts it plainly: "their informality of wording and phrase was built into the text", and "The President appeared to talk with his listeners rather than lecturing at them." The first talk, on 12 March 1933, was delivered from the Diplomatic Reception Room with the President actually sitting next to a fireplace. The room is the argument: he is somewhere specific, you are somewhere specific, and the distance between them is being described rather than hidden.

The name came later and from somebody else. The Library of Congress credits Washington broadcast executive Harry Butcher with it "on the occasion of the second one"; the Roosevelt library says the term "was not coined by FDR" but by a reporter describing the speech of 7 May 1933. Both are kept, because both are compatible and because neither makes it his. **The form is famous under a name its author did not choose**, which is the correct outcome for a form built out of other people's living rooms.

The count is honestly open and says so: "There was no solid definition as to what constituted a Fireside Chat. As a result, there is some dispute as to the total number of Fireside Chats that FDR delivered." The Library of Congress has the range at between twenty-seven and thirty-one, the last in June 1944. **A form people recognise before a committee defines it is a form, and a form with a number attached is a list.** The dispute is not a defect in the record; it is the record of something that was defined by being listened to.

What it was for is in the mechanics. All the national radio networks carried them - hundreds of stations nationwide - opening with "my friends" and, the first time, with "I want to talk for a few minutes with the people of the United States about banking...". That sentence assumes you are already there and already listening; "my friends" is not a form of address but a claim about the relationship, made by an office that held the whole schedule. The first talk "was credited with averting widespread panic." **Nobody in the audience could answer, and that is not a flaw in the design.** It is the design, applied on purpose, by a government that had decided the thing to do next was to be in the room with you.

src.citation: Christopher H. Sterling, essay on the fireside chats, National Recording Preservation Board, Library of Congress (PDF)
src.claim: The naming, the first talk, and the three quotations the entry is built on. That "These 'Fireside Chats' (so named by Washington broadcast executive Harry Butcher on the occasion of the second one) were planned as conversations rather than stiff public speeches."; that they were carried by all the national radio networks, meaning hundreds of stations nationwide; that "most agree that between 27 and 31 were broadcast by the time of the last one in June, 1944"; that the first chat was delivered on March 12, 1933 from the Diplomatic Reception Room "with the President actually sitting next to a fireplace"; that "The talk was credited with averting widespread panic."; that "their informality of wording and phrase was built into the text"; and that "The President appeared to talk with his listeners rather than lecturing at them." Also the opening of the first talk, "I want to talk for a few minutes with the people of the United States about banking...", and the customary opening, "my friends". nodes.s: The first documented fan clubs, organised around sheet music and radio rather than film. Following became joining.
nodes.g: The behaviour did not arrive with any technology. It arrived with the possibility of being heard, and a great deal of organisation, done unpaid, by people who were young.

nodes.s: Persistent text spaces with per-topic cultures, norms enforced by social pressure and volume.
nodes.g: Where the pile-on was invented. Fandom moved from letters to threads, and a thread has thousands of people in it at once with no moderator and no cost to replying.

nodes.s: A relationship with a competitor offered free while a subscription relationship is locked in behind the same login.
nodes.g: Platforms discovered that a user will defend the platform they have a relationship with against the platform offering them a better deal. The parasocial bond is now a competitive moat, and it is documented as such in the filings.

src.claim: The free trial as a documented pattern rather than an anecdote: Hidden Subscription is defined as charging a recurring fee under the pretense of a one-time fee or a free trial, and users often learn of it only days or months later

nodes.g: Historians use it as a mark of how far the field has moved. Almost nothing in the current literature treats the viewer as strange. The interesting correction is not that gazing is normal but that the frame itself was the problem - one person studied, the other one an object.

nodes.s: The song where the singer pleads to be given the exact shape a man wants: a French phrase, a café in the dark. A whole musical built around wanting to be a specific imaginary person for somebody.
nodes.g: The template for a large fraction of the twentieth century. Cole Porter did not invent the impulse, he published it, and the song is still the most precise description of the thing that every subsequent song about obsessive attachment is a worse version of.

nodes.s: Round enclosures on a hillside in Anatolia holding T-shaped pillars carved to suggest human figures, built by people who had not yet domesticated a single animal - used for over a thousand years, then deliberately filled in and built over.
nodes.g: The oldest thing on this site with a claim to be about figures, and the interpretation is genuinely open, which is the point. What is not in dispute: hunter-gatherers cut limestone into anthropomorphic forms with stone and bone tools, set them upright in circles, carved them with foxes, scorpions, lions and vultures, returned to them for fourteen hundred years, and then filled the enclosures in on purpose. There is no hearth, no rubbish pit and no sign that anyone lived there - people travelled to the place. UNESCO's own nomination describes the pillars as believed to represent 'ancestors, perhaps even incipient deities', and other readings have them as totemic or protective figures. Nobody has settled it, and the carvings include a great many frightening animals: the dominant imagery is not a kind face but lions, spiders, snakes and scorpions. What this site can claim is narrow and still large: for at least a millennium, people made representations of beings, went out of their way to be near them, and eventually chose to close the place where they stood. Whether the beings were ancestors is the question this entry cannot answer, and saying so is more useful here than guessing.

src.claim: Dating, construction and the absence of settlement: the structures are among the earliest evidence worldwide for human-made megalithic buildings constructed specifically for the ritual requirements of their prehistoric population, erected between approximately 9600 and 8200 BC in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, some 6,000 years before Stonehenge. The T-shaped pillars 'embodying a schematised anthropomorphic figure' were carved from the adjacent limestone plateau with stone and bone tools. The enclosures were probably used for public rituals, possibly of a funerary nature, and feasting.
src.citation: Göbekli Tepe (Turkey), No 1572: nomination and evaluation. UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 2018.

src.claim: The interpretive status, in the words of the nominating body, and the deliberate closure: 'The anthropomorphic T-shaped pillars are believed to be representations of ancestors, perhaps even incipient deities.' The enclosures of Layer III were then 'intentionally backfilled', the fills containing numerous animal bones 'probably the result of large feasts'.
src.citation: Executive Summary, Göbekli Tepe (Turkey), No 1572. UNESCO World Heritage Centre.

src.claim: That it was a place people travelled to rather than lived: the remains of undomesticated plant material and tens of thousands of wild animal bones - chiefly gazelle - were recovered, 'but the lack of trash pits, hearths, or other signals of domestic life indicates that it was most likely not a permanent settlement'; most experts identify it as a ritual site 'that may have attracted worshipers from great distances'. First investigated in the 1960s and dismissed as a medieval cemetery before its true age was established in the 1990s.
src.citation: Gobekli Tepe. Encyclopaedia Britannica.

src.claim: Site description and the imagery: circular enclosures each containing two large T-shaped pillars ringed by smaller stones facing inward, the tallest around 16 feet and up to 50 tons; carvings including foxes, scorpions, lions, vultures and other wild animals; site known by the Turkish name meaning 'belly hill'.
src.citation: Göbekli Tepe. Wikipedia.

nodes.s: A recurring family, played by the same cast, five nights a week, for years, in a house you could draw from memory.
nodes.g: Attachment to a fictional household, watched nightly, in the pre-internet equivalent of a comfort rewatch. Research on sitcom parasocial attachment found the same pattern as soaps: it is the accumulation, not the plot.

src.claim: N=840: appreciation and enjoyment are separate responses. Appreciation is being moved; enjoyment is pleasure. Tragic outcomes still produce appreciation even where enjoyment is absent - the family you miss was never the fun one
src.citation: Krakowiak, K. M. (2024). How It Ends: Exploring How Narrative Closure and Character Outcomes in Series Finales Relate to Viewer Responses and Coping Behaviors.

src.claim: And the mechanism that makes loss social: appreciation INCREASED coping behaviours - seeking more information, reading analyses, discussing with other viewers - while enjoyment decreased them. Feeling moved makes you go and talk to someone
src.citation: Krakowiak, K. M. (2024). How It Ends.

nodes.s: Six million people remain in a public argument about characters who no longer exist, for years, entirely in good faith.
nodes.g: A parasocial relationship conducted in public with complete strangers, where nobody is pretending and everybody is sincere. It is also the largest documented instance of viewers disagreeing about a shared fiction as if it were a shared fact.

src.claim: 'The Iron Throne', 19 May 2019, became the least-watched episode of the series it finished - a finale whose audience was actively hostile to it, and whose coffee cups became a small consumer-protection story
src.citation: The Iron Throne (Game of Thrones) (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: A national loyalty scheme in Britain, redeemed for goods, with a book of stamps kept in the house.
nodes.g: The first loyalty programme most families would have lived with for a generation, and a physical object in the home. The customer's book of stamps is an account balance that lives in a cupboard, which is a genius piece of interface design that nobody has beaten.

src.claim: Launched in the United Kingdom in 1958, Green Shield Stamps is among the longest-running trading-stamp loyalty schemes and remains in circulation decades later. The card outlived most of the shops that issued it
src.citation: Green Shield Stamps (Wikipedia).

nodes.t: Grieving a person you never met
nodes.s: Collective mourning of a public figure, and the persistent argument about whether it counts. Measured in studies of soap opera finales finding grief markers the same shape as the end of a relationship.
nodes.g: The largest and most defensible category on this site. Losing somebody is what happens when the people you love die, and a very large number of people grieve in public and are told it is a symptom. The only unusual thing about parasocial grief is that the person could not have known you were there, and that deserves care rather than condescension.

src.claim: Parasocial grief is real, measurable, and specifically disenfranchised: a death the world does not recognise as a loss
src.citation: DeGroot, J. M., & Leith, A. P. (2018). R.I.P. Kutner: Parasocial Grief Following the Death of a Television Character. Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly, 77(3), 199-216.

src.claim: Grief at the end of a long series, measured at scale (n=1289) after the Neighbours finale
src.citation: Gerace, A. (2024). When TV neighbours become good friends: Understanding Neighbours fans' feelings of grief and loss at the end of the series. PLOS ONE.

src.claim: Character death and series cancellation produce similar distress; voluntary withdrawal produces much less
