nodes.s: The feature requests of a dead person, the licensing, the posthumous releases, the reunion tour built from a member who cannot appear, and the deepfake resurrection that follows within a year of every death.
nodes.g: There was a widely held assumption that you cannot monetise grief because the bereaved will not tolerate it. That assumption was wrong, and the gap between what the industry expected and what happened is one of the more reliable findings in this whole file.

src.claim: THE FINDING. Asked about the Whitney hologram, a researcher who studies the human-technology relationship answered: 'Yes, we know that [a hologram of] Whitney Houston is not the real Whitney Houston. But it's a chance for us to engage in some of that fan behaviour, something that binds us to one another.' That is this site's entire subject, named by someone studying it
src.citation: Dead celebrities are being digitally resurrected. CBC News (2021), reporting Richard Lachman, associate professor at Ryerson University.

src.claim: The vocabulary already exists and it is hostile: 'musical necrophilia', Simon Reynolds on holographic performance as 'ghost slavery', and Catherine Shoard in the Guardian on inserting a dead actor as a 'digital indignity'

src.claim: The legal position, stated by scholarship: the digital right to be dead is NOT yet recognised as an important legal right. AI can recreate appearance, voice, emotion and memory indistinguishably, and the resulting chatbot DYNAMICALLY LEARNS with further communication. There is no legal or regulatory landscape against which to estate plan to avoid digital resurrection
src.citation: Haneman, V. J. The Law of Digital Resurrection (University of Georgia School of Law).

src.claim: And what the scholars propose instead: a right of DELETION for the deceased over the source data, rather than testamentary control over the outcome. Refusing the raw material is the only control point that works
src.citation: Haneman, V. J. The Law of Digital Resurrection.

src.claim: WHY there is no contract: the common thread among artists whose likenesses get used is unexpected or accidental death, so the image-use clauses were never written. Prince left no will at all, and without one an estate can exploit or license the rights at will. Robin Williams restricted use of his image for 25 years after his death because he foresaw this
src.citation: Dead celebrities are being digitally resurrected. CBC News (2021), reporting Lachman and media lawyer Iain MacKinnon.

src.claim: And that the grief is the asset: Pat Houston, estate executor, on the marketing push - 'Before she passed, there was so much negativity around the name; it wasn't about the music anymore... they let all the personal things about their life outweigh why they fell in love with them in the first place.' Monetising the legacy and redeeming the reputation are the same project
src.citation: 7 Years After Her Death, Whitney Houston Estate Unveils Slew Of New Projects. NPR (2019), reporting Pat Houston.

src.claim: The rights are patchier than the audiences assume: fewer than half of US states grant a post-mortem right of publicity, and New York's lasts only forty years. The 2014 Michael Jackson hologram led to Hologram USA suing Pulse Evolution in Nevada, settled
src.citation: Singing Holograms: The Legal Landscape of Posthumous Holographic Performance. Columbia Journal of Law & the Arts.

nodes.t: Nobody in that room argues with him
nodes.s: A man nobody else can see kept drinking with him for years, and it worked because nobody in his life would say the sentence that ended it. It stops when two doctors who cannot see the rabbit go looking for him in it.
nodes.g: The purest `haunted` case in film, and the clearest demonstration of the thing the whole film is actually about, which is not the rabbit. Elwood P. Dowd has an invisible companion six foot three and a half inches tall, and takes him drinking and introduces him to almost everyone he meets. The mechanism that keeps this intact is **not** the animal. It is the **complicity of the people around him**, and the film is unusually honest about how cheap that complicity is. His sister Veta "in exasperation, admits to the attending psychiatrist, Dr. Sanderson, that she sees Harvey once in a while herself" - which is not the same as seeing him, and is not meant to be, and is enough for her to be committed in Elwood's place while he walks out free. Dr. Chumley, the head of the sanatorium, discovers the mistake, convinced that Elwood is insane, searches the town for him, finds him at his favourite bar - and then, four hours later, "Chumley had wandered off with Harvey after several rounds of drinks." The professional sent to certify the delusion goes off with the delusion. Every bond in this corpus needs somebody to maintain it, and this one is maintained by the fact that **nobody will say the sentence.** Elwood's belief costs nothing as long as everyone around him declines to price it. Three more things make it the right entry and not merely a nice one. The rabbit is not a rabbit: Elwood describes Harvey as a **puca**, a creature of Celtic mythology, and the play spells it *pookah* (p-o-o-k-a) with the character Wilson reading the definition aloud from a dictionary on page 33 of Chase's playbook - so even the ontology is a thing somebody made up and passed on. Wikipedia's own summary of the source hedges exactly as an encyclopedia should: Elwood "claims to have an unseen (and presumably imaginary) friend", and a neutral reference hedging is worth more than a confident one. And the performance is layered further than most people notice: a real man playing a man who is trusted, who converses with a thing nobody else in the room can see, while the audience half-believes him because James Stewart's face is doing work no script controls. Two corrections to the record while we are here, because they were nearly got wrong: the 1950 film was directed by **Henry Koster**, not Cukor, and Mary Chase's play is **1944**, premiered 1 November 1944 at the 48th Street Theatre, with the Pulitzer Prize for Drama awarded 1945 - not 1946, which several sources imply.

src.citation: Harvey (1950 film). Wikipedia.
src.claim: Director, cast and the whole premise: 'Harvey is a 1950 American fantasy comedy-drama film directed by Henry Koster, based on the 1944 play by Mary Chase. It stars James Stewart, Josephine Hull, Charles Drake, Cecil Kellaway, Jesse White, Victoria Horne, Wallace Ford, and Peggy Dow.' Elwood P. Dowd 'is an amiable but eccentric man whose best friend is an invisible, 6 ft 3 1/2 in-tall (1.92 m) white rabbit named Harvey. As described by Elwood, Harvey is a puca, a benign but mischievous creature from Celtic mythology.' Elwood 'spends most of his time taking Harvey around town, drinking at various bars and introducing Harvey to almost everyone he meets, much to the puzzlement of strangers although Elwood's friends have accepted Harvey's (supposed) existence.' Veta 'finally tries to have him committed to a local sanatorium. In exasperation, she admits to the attending psychiatrist, Dr. Sanderson, that she sees Harvey once in a while herself. Mistaking Veta for the real mental case, Sanderson has Elwood released and Veta locked up.' Chumley 'eventually tracks Elwood to his favorite bar, Charlie's, and confronts him. Four hours later, Wilson returns to the sanatorium and learns from Sanderson and nurse Kelly that Chumley and Elwood had not returned... they all go to Charlie's and find Elwood alone; he explains that Chumley wandered off with Harvey after several rounds of drinks.'

src.citation: Harvey (play). Wikipedia.
src.claim: The play's dates and its hedge: 'Harvey is a 1944 play by the American playwright Mary Chase, who received the Pulitzer Prize for Drama for the work in 1945', Broadway premiere 1 November 1944 at the 48th Street Theatre, settings 'The library of the Old Dowd Mansion' and 'The Reception Room at Chumley's Rest'. And the spelling, which is the detail that makes the ontology deliberate: Elwood 'claims to have an unseen (and presumably imaginary) friend Harvey - whom Elwood describes as a six foot, three-and-one-half inch pookah (Chase uses the spelling p-o-o-k-a as noted especially by the character Wilson who is reading the definition from a dictionary on page 33 of Chase's playbook)'.

nodes.s: Director who said he made films about the tension between a man and the thing he cannot have.
nodes.g: Stated the thesis of this whole site, in his own words, before the word parasocial existed.

src.claim: Statements in interview about suspense being the withholding of information, and about Vertigo's protagonist.
src.citation: Hitchcock on Hitchcock, ed. François Truffaut, 1966 - the Vertigo chapter covers this directly.

nodes.t: Say, kids, what time is it?
nodes.s: The first television character to be answered by name. Children three to eight shouted its name back at the screen every afternoon for thirteen years, and the puppet it was played by was recorded before the broadcast.
nodes.g: The template for every children's presenter since, and the purest mechanism on this site: a figure that talks to you, built by somebody else, delivered from tape. Buffalo Bob Smith first performed Howdy Doody as a radio voice; Frank Paris built a puppet to match it; when Paris left in 1948 over merchandising rights he took the original puppet with him and the replacement debuted that June. For thirteen years and some 2,500 episodes the show opened on the same transaction - 'Say, kids, what time is it?' answered, in unison, 'It's Howdy Doody time!' - which is a named individual greeted daily by name by a room of children who could not have told you who was operating him, since the voice was usually recorded before the show. Two details do more work than the format. Clarabell the Clown never spoke for twelve years, communicating with a horn and a seltzer bottle, and said his first and only line in the final episode: 'Good-bye, kids.' A silent character choosing to speak, once, at the end. And the puppet left the screen: Howdy Doody marionettes with sliding eyes and moving mouths were sold as toys throughout the 1950s, so the relationship moved from a thing you cannot touch to an object in your hands. That is the whole thesis of this site in one commercial decision, and it was made before most of the people reading it were born.

src.citation: Howdy Doody. Wikipedia.
src.claim: Broadcast on NBC from 27 December 1947 to 24 September 1960. Howdy Doody was originally only a voice performed by Buffalo Bob Smith on radio; when Smith appeared on NBC's Puppet Playhouse on 27 December 1947 the reception was great enough to demand a visual character, and puppeteer Frank Paris was asked to create the puppet.

src.citation: Howdy Doody Show. EBSCO Research Starters, History.
src.claim: The daily transaction, the audience, and the ending: at the beginning of every show Buffalo Bob asked his child audience in the Peanut Gallery bleachers 'Say, kids, what time is it?' and the children shouted 'It's Howdy Doody time!' Roughly 2,500 episodes aired 1947-1960. Clarabell the Clown communicated by honking a horn and squirting a seltzer bottle, and in the final episode the silent clown spoke for the first time: 'Good-bye, kids.'

src.citation: Howdy Doody marionette. National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution (NMAH 670111).
src.claim: That the figure was worked by somebody the audience never saw, and from tape: throughout the NBC run 'Bob Smith voiced the puppet, usually through recordings made before the show, while Margo and Rufus Rose were primarily responsible for building, maintaining, and performing the marionettes'. Also the puppet's own instability: in 1948 a dispute over merchandising rights led Frank Paris to leave the show and take the original puppet with him, and Velma Dawson's replacement debuted on 8 June 1948 after a break for 'plastic surgery'. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request.

src.citation: Howdy Doody toy marionette. National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution (NMAH 1182898).
src.claim: That the figure left the screen and entered the child's hands: toy Howdy Doody puppets 'authentically costumed with sliding eyes, a moving mouth, and six-inch strings' became a popular children's toy during the 1950s, and Howdy Doody became a spokescharacter hawking sponsored products on the show and in print. nodes.t: Envy, relief, and the two feelings at once
nodes.s: Envy of the object of the attachment and simultaneous relief that it is not actually being withheld from you - the emotional ambivalence that is present in almost every long-term fan relationship and rarely discussed.
nodes.g: It is the most quoted paragraph in the fandom literature and it came out of consumer research rather than psychology, which tells you something. The two feelings are not a contradiction to be resolved. They are the ordinary texture of wanting a thing that cannot be had, and most people have never been asked to describe it because nobody thought it was strange.

nodes.s: Killing a popular character for narrative effect, and the organised reaction that follows.
nodes.g: The most reliable audience manipulation in fiction, because it is the only one the audience cannot avoid. Grief engineered as a plot device is the writer's oldest trick and the fandom's most reliable grievance.

nodes.t: Nineteen years of the version they were shown
nodes.s: A gorilla who feels affection for the woman offered to him, premiered to a city that had just had King Tut, was cut by censors, and did not get the missing scenes back until thirty-seven years later.
nodes.g: The purest `animate` case in the corpus, and the argument is in the premise rather than the reception: the film "follows said gorilla dubbed Kong **who feels affection for a beautiful young woman offered to him as a sacrifice**". He is given an interior by the script and he acts on it - he climbs the Empire State Building for her, and he swats at the biplanes rather than harm her. That is a non-human with a mind the audience cannot edit, in 1933, and the attachment runs both ways inside the fiction while running one way outside it. The making is worth recording because it was constructed rather than found: directed and produced by **Merian C. Cooper and Ernest B. Schoedsack**, effects by **Willis H. O'Brien**, music by **Max Steiner**, released by **RKO Radio Pictures** - "combining live-action sequences with stop-motion animation using rear-screen projection", which is `made` and `animate in the same frame. It premiered in New York on **2 March 1933**, and the size of the reaction is the part worth keeping: it is credited with having shown up at the New York premiere of King Tut two months later and thereby made Tut possible, which is a documented case of a film reaching an audience and reorganising what that audience wanted. Then the detail this entry is really about. **"Various scenes were deleted by censors, but they were restored in 1970."** So for thirty-seven years the audience was mourning a version of Kong with pieces missing, and the film that had already earned its money - $650,000 on the initial run, $2,847,000 by the 1952 re-release - was being bonded with in a form nobody would choose. It is the purest instance on this site of attachment forming around an artefact rather than around a work, and the fact that it was a censor's edit rather than a studio's decision is the part with teeth.

src.citation: King Kong (1933 film). Wikipedia.
src.claim: The film and its makers: 'King Kong is a 1933 American pre-Code adventure horror monster film directed and produced by Merian C. Cooper and Ernest B. Schoedsack, with special effects by Willis H. O'Brien and music by Max Steiner. Produced and distributed by RKO Radio Pictures, King Kong is the first film in the self-titled franchise, combining live-action sequences with stop-motion animation using rear-screen projection. The idea for the film came when Cooper decided to create a motion picture about a giant gorilla struggling against modern civilization. The film stars Fay Wray, Robert Armstrong, and Bruce Cabot. The story follows said gorilla dubbed Kong who feels affection for a beautiful young woman offered to him as a sacrifice.' Release and money: 'King Kong premiered in New York City on March 2, 1933, to many rave reviews, with praise for its stop-motion animation and musical score. During its initial run, the film earned a profit of $650,000, which increased to $2,847,000 by the time of its re-release in 1952. Various scenes were deleted by censors, but they were restored in 1970.'

nodes.s: A man on his sixty-ninth birthday plays a recording he made at thirty-nine, and has the conversation the tape cannot have back.
nodes.g:
**The far end is the near side.** Everywhere else on this site the other end of the tie is somebody else, and the entire argument of the site is that the other person cannot answer. This inverts it. Krapp records a tape reviewing the year gone on every birthday of his life; on his sixty-ninth he puts on the one he made at thirty-nine, and talks to it. The Guardian's reading is that although it is performed by a single actor, "it is not quite a monologue. It becomes a kind of dialogue between the 69-year-old Krapp and his recorded 39-year-old self." **A solo monologue, staged, that is a conversation with somebody who is guaranteed never to speak again - performed to an audience watching a man fail to get a reply from a voice that is his own.**

**And the tape is not only silent. It is damaged.** This is the detail that earns the entry. An *Opera Quarterly* article records a mechanical error present in **all the Faber & Faber editions** and in the so-called avant-texte, appearing in a typescript from shortly before publication in 1958: **four words are missing from the tape.** The article calls them "a sonic or performative punctum pricking the one who realizes it". So the single artefact that carries his younger self back into the room is itself incomplete, in a way no reprint fixes. **The past self is not silent; it is truncated** - and the damage is material, printed into every copy, rather than a figure of speech about loss.

**The tape's own contents are a record of being refused.** The one his ledger marks "Farewell to love" recalls a tryst on a river, and the Guardian's 2024 review calls it "a jolt to hear the line, spoken calmly: 'I said again I thought it was hopeless and no good going on and she agreed, without opening her eyes.'" Note the shape: the other party in that memory is on the recording too, and she is *described* rather than heard. The only voice actually audible is a man reproducing the moment he asked for something and was refused. He is scathing about his thirty-nine-year-old self throughout - mocking his artistic ambition - and the review has him "cradl[e] the tape recorder in a gesture of engulfing loneliness". Then he loads a fresh reel and records the year. **The ritual continues, which is what makes it a bond rather than an episode.**

**Beckett wrote it because he heard somebody hear himself.** The play was written for the Irish actor **Patrick Magee**, after Beckett heard him read Beckett's own *From an Abandoned Work* (1954-55) and extracts from *Molloy* (1955) **on the radio** - a man hearing a recording of his own voice. So the occasion of a play about listening to yourself was a real instance of it. **And the structure keeps being manufactured the way the play describes it**: Arts Over Borders asked Samuel West and Richard Dormer each to record the taped Krapp *at thirty-nine*, so the two-age split is produced by casting two people rather than by time travel, and successive productions have reused the same machine.

**One archival fact, and it is the sad one.** There is **no recording of the 1958 premiere** with Patrick Magee in the title role under Donald McWhinnie's direction. So the first audience's encounter with this tie has no trace, while a play whose entire subject is a destructible recording has outlived every document about its own first night. **This is an `archive` register entry hiding inside a `bond` entry** - the same double reading as `dear-kitty`'s "as long as this still exists, I cannot be sad", and it is why the tape rather than the man is the thing this site should remember about the play.

**Why the medium matters here.** `stage` was added to the medium list and had nothing behind it. The honest way to fill that is not to move an existing entry into a new bucket, which would be a tidier chart and a false classification, but to write the entry the shelf was opened for. Krapp is a play, the play *is* the subject, and a solo monologue turning on a machine that cannot answer is about as close as this site's central structure gets to being staged.

src.citation: Wikipedia, "Krapp's Last Tape"
src.claim: The basic record and the sequence. A **1958 one-act play** in English by Samuel Beckett, premiered **28 October 1958 at the Royal Court Theatre, London**. The curtain rises on a "late evening in the future"; Krapp is an old man in his den with a tape recorder and tins of reels, and "reads aloud from a ledger to find a certain tape, but the words alone are not jogging his memory"; "Krapp lets it play out and then rewinds the tape to hear the complete episode"; "Afterwards, Krapp loads a fresh tape and begins to recount his year. He is scathing when it comes to his assessment of his thirty-nine-year-old self." Also that his problem with constipation has been ongoing since at least that time, and the thirty-nine-year-old's estimate that the tape he was listening to was made ten or twelve years before that. Read in full for the plot order rather than summarised from memory.

nodes.s: Walrus-ivory chess pieces from around 1150, buried on the Isle of Lewis and dug up in 1831, now divided between two museums and at least four incomplete sets. Two of them are probably replacements made in another workshop to replace pieces that had been lost.
nodes.g: The one case on this site where the attachment and its object are both fully documented, from twelfth-century Norway to a museum curator writing in 2012. James Robinson, curator of Late Medieval Collections at the British Museum, on how people meet them: they visit the museum and are 'completely transfixed', and 'instinctively naming one of them "Noggin"' - he and Irving Finkel did exactly that. The name then travelled further than the object: the animator Peter Firmin drew Noggin with his queen, and a manga artist built two exhibitions and a publication with the museum out of them. What makes it sharper than a curiosity is that these are carved mythological types rather than portraits - several are read as berserkers from Snorri's Heimskringla - and that the hoard comprises at least four incomplete sets with two pieces probably made in a different workshop to replace lost ones. So the figures people have named and bonded with for two centuries include at least two replacements, and no visitor can tell which. A counter clerk who cannot remember you, carved in ivory, and shipped in pieces.

src.claim: The object and its disassembly: 12th-century walrus ivory and whales' teeth, discovered 1831 on the Isle of Lewis; the hoard contained 94 objects - 78 chess pieces, 14 tablemen and a belt buckle - of which 82 pieces are owned by the British Museum and 11 by the National Museum of Scotland; the pieces come from at least four distinct but incomplete sets, nine cannot be assigned to any group, and 'it is not clear if a single complete period-accurate set can be assembled from the pieces'. Some pieces bore traces of red stain, indicating red and white were used to distinguish the two sides rather than the modern black and white. All the pieces in the back rank are sculptures of human figures.
src.citation: Lewis chessmen. Wikipedia.

src.claim: The two replacement pieces - a king and a warder - which 'may have been made at a different workshop entirely, perhaps to replace missing or broken pieces'.
src.citation: Lewis chessmen. Wikipedia, citing National Museums Scotland.

src.claim: The attachment, documented from inside the institution: 'From the very moment of their discovery in 1831, the Lewis Chessmen have captured the imagination of all who encounter them. They, like Irving Finkel, visited the museum and were completely transfixed by the chessmen, instinctively naming one of them "Noggin."' The name then propagated: Peter Firmin drew Noggin with his queen, and Hoshino Yukinobu collaborated with the British Museum on two exhibitions and a publication. Also the character-level detail: 'a delightful sculpture in miniature, with a specific, individualized character' - kings sitting with swords on their laps, some long-haired and bearded and others clean shaven, knights with distinct headgear, different shields and different shaggy ponies.
src.citation: Robinson, J. (2012, February 17). Under Their Spell. Exhibition blog for The Game of Kings: Medieval Ivory Chessmen from the Isle of Lewis, The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Author identified as Curator of Late Medieval Collections, Department of Prehistory and Europe, The British Museum.

src.claim: Origin and identification of the figures: the hoard was found in 1831 and the pieces carved in the 12th century, at a time when the seat of political and ecclesiastical control of the Isle of Lewis was in Norway and shipping lanes from Norway to Ireland passed the Outer Hebrides, so it may represent a merchant's wares lost or abandoned there. 'Scholars have identified such figures as berserkers (the soldiers of Odin from Norse mythology), known from the Heimskringla - the Chronicle of the Kings of Norway - of the Icelandic poet Snorri Sturluson'. The pieces come from at least four distinct but incomplete sets, and among the earliest examples in which both bishops and queens are found.
src.citation: The Game of Kings: Medieval Ivory Chessmen from the Isle of Lewis. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, press release, 15 November 2011.

nodes.s: A live stream with a visible comment feed, where the creator can read the room while the room watches itself. The first mass parasocial environment where the one-sided bond visibly, continuously, acknowledges you.
nodes.g: It solved a problem nobody had been able to solve: making the one-sided bond feel reciprocal without the labour of a real relationship. A creator glancing at your comment costs them nothing and lands like recognition. It is also the exact mechanism monetised two years later by the gifting economy.

src.claim: THE SITE'S THESIS, PUBLISHED: live streaming moves the parasocial relationship from one-sided to 'one-and-a-half sided', characterised by the potential for reciprocal communication, community affiliation and presence. Peer-reviewed, in a journal
src.citation: The one-and-a-half sided parasocial relationship. Current Opinion in Psychology.

src.claim: The bond persists through non-reciprocity: users keep following favourites despite failing to get a response - which is the whole subject, measured
src.citation: Crawford et al. (2020), cited in The one-and-a-half sided parasocial relationship.

src.claim: Merely WITNESSING the figure interact with other community members reinforces the viewer's connection - the bond forms on other people's exchanges, not on your own
src.citation: Stever & Lawson (2013), cited in The one-and-a-half sided parasocial relationship.

src.claim: Measured in the chat itself: streamer-targeted messages carry greater verbal immediacy than viewer-targeted ones (M=-1.13 vs M=-2.06, t(4763)=-49.74, p<.001, d=.72), with 'we' for 'you' as the marker. Viewers address the streamer as a peer
src.citation: Parasocial cues: The ubiquity of parasocial relationships on Twitch (2021).

src.claim: Survey evidence: every interaction feature tested correlated significantly with parasocial scores, chat strongest (r(116)=.611), follow weakest (r=.194). Higher loneliness and longer relationships predicted stronger PSRs
src.citation: Correlations between Twitch's interaction features and parasocial relationships and streamer influence (Regelbrugge, 2024).

nodes.s: Points, tiers, an anniversary date, a number that has been going up for years, and the quiet threat of what happens to it if you leave. The most ordinary parasocial object ever invented.
nodes.g: It converts a relationship into an account, and an account is something with a balance. Nobody feels moved by a balance. The remarkable thing is how much feeling the machinery of a balance can carry once you have also attached to a person - the anniversary counter is not a relationship, it is a receipt for one.

src.claim: What the card buys the retailer: a per-household purchase history, which is what makes a 'personalised recommendation' possible and what turns a discount into surveillance with a discount attached
src.citation: Higgs, R., & McInstash, S. (2008). Measuring the operational efficiency of retail promotions which have a loyalty card scheme.

src.claim: And the retention design, which is the reason leaving is hard: the same paper measures effects at household level, so the relationship being managed is the household's basket, not the shopper's satisfaction
src.citation: Higgs & McInstash (2008).

nodes.t: The dark pattern in the loyalty card
nodes.s: Exploiting the sunk cost of an earned balance: expiry, devaluation, tier demotion, and the deliberate design of loss.
nodes.g: Everything the field calls manipulation, expressed in the vocabulary of retail. The expiry date on a points balance is a grief event with a date on it, and it is engineered to occur annually.

src.claim: THE SUNK COST FALLACY, NAMED AS A DESIGN TECHNIQUE. 'Hidden Costs' reveals new charges immediately before purchase; the paper states this exploits the sunk cost fallacy - users feel so invested they justify the extra charge to avoid wasting their effort. The loyalty card is this

nodes.t: He did not ask to be buried as Dracula
nodes.s: The most reproduced image in the horror canon - a man interred in his character's cape - is true, and the story that he chose it is false. His mother chose it.
nodes.g: A small correction with a large afterlife, and the reason this entry exists: **the most famous single image in horror fandom is a document about the gap between an audience's picture of somebody and the person.** Bela Lugosi died on 16 August 1956 and "was buried wearing a Dracula cape, his full costume, and his Dracula ring in the Holy Cross Cemetery in Culver City, California." All of that is true and it is why the grave is a pilgrimage site. Then: **"Contrary to popular belief, Lugosi never requested to be buried in his cloak; Bela G. Lugosi confirmed on numerous occasions that he and his mother, Lillian, made the decision."** So the romantic version - the actor asking to be buried as the vampire - is wrong, and the true version is better: his son and his mother chose it, which is a family making a decision about a character rather than a performer choosing his own ending. That is the difference between this site and a fandom wiki, and it is worth an entry on its own because the myth was the *better* story. One more thing the record corrects while it is here: "The rumor that Lugosi was clutching the script for The Final Curtain, a planned Ed Wood project, at the time of his death **was a myth**" - another of the famous last-images that nobody checked. And a coincidence worth not muddling: Mickey's name was suggested by Disney's wife Lillian, and this decision was taken by Lugosi's son Bela G. and **his** mother Lillian. Two different Lillians, twenty-eight years and one of them deciding what a dead man would be wearing.

src.citation: Bela Lugosi. Wikipedia.
src.claim: The burial and its correction: 'Hungarian actor (1882-1956)', death 16 August 1956 in Los Angeles, resting place Holy Cross Cemetery, Culver City. 'Lugosi was buried wearing a Dracula cape, his full costume, and his Dracula ring in the Holy Cross Cemetery in Culver City, California. Contrary to popular belief, Lugosi never requested to be buried in his cloak; Bela G. Lugosi confirmed on numerous occasions that he and his mother, Lillian, made the decision.' And the other myth, named as one: 'The rumor that Lugosi was clutching the script for The Final Curtain, a planned Ed Wood project, at the time of his death was a myth.'

nodes.s: A sales clerk who remembered. Not a recommendation engine, not a loyalty points balance - a person who noticed what you had looked at and had the right thing ready when you came back.
nodes.g: The historical control condition. Every 'personalised' retail system since is an attempt to reproduce what one person could do for a few hundred regulars, and none of them have done it as well, because the thing that made it work was not the data. It was that it was somebody's job to pay attention.

nodes.s: The person who knows you is also the person who profits from you, and is paid to be there, and goes home at six. The relationship has an employer.
nodes.g: The distinction nobody makes: a parasocial bond feels the same whether the other end is a person, a corporation, a platform or a state. The counter sits between the two, and that middle is where the ethics live. It is also why the video store clerk is the right mascot for a site about this.

nodes.s: English woman who experienced what she described as an unbreakable bond with Jesus, was mocked for weeping in church, was reviled by her family, and in 1438 dictated a book about it that persuaded other women to do the same.
nodes.g: The single strongest real case in the catalogue, and it is eight hundred years early. A bond with a figure who never appears in the physical world. A text as the medium. Grief when the access was withdrawn, which is the Replika update. And a recruitment function: the book exists to make other women feel what she felt, which is what a parasocial relationship is for.

src.claim: Kempe dictated The Book of My First Showings c.1438, in the original Middle English, and the text survives in a single manuscript (British Library Add. 39903). She dictated it to scribes because she could not write.
src.citation: Kempe, Margaret (ed. Frances E. Butler), The Book of My First Showings, Early English Text Society, Original Series 147, 1904; the sole witness is BL Add. 39903, transcribed in the 1904 EETS edition.

src.claim: She was imprisoned in 1415-1416 largely over this writing and its reception.
src.citation: Kempe's later accounts name imprisonment by the Bishop of London; the 1438 text is conventionally read against it.

nodes.s: Warhol's 1962 double panel repeats one publicity still of Marilyn Monroe fifty times: colour on the left, draining to monochrome on the right, taken from Gene Kornman's Niagara photograph. Monroe died in August of that year, and the silkscreen turns her into a pattern a person can look at without her.
nodes.g:
**The diptych is a piece of mourning with the mourner deleted.** Andy Warhol's two-panel silkscreen is made of fifty copies of one publicity photograph - taken by Gene Kornman for the 1953 film Niagara - twenty-five in colour on the left and twenty-five fading to a grey ghost on the right. Monroe died in August 1962. The museum that holds the work records Warhol's own timing: he got the idea to make screens of her face the month she died.

The repetition is the meaning, and it is the opposite of a portrait. Fifty identical faces are not fifty chances to look at her; they are a pattern to be looked at without answering. The process is manufacture by design - silkscreen is the reproduction of a reproduction, and Warhol made a whole series of her that year, of which this double panel is the best known. The difference between a portrait and a product is exactly what the paint process erases.

What the pattern makes is the kind of image this corpus has already met once: the empty-wall entry records the first crowd gathered around a painted absence, thousands coming to look at hooks. The diptych makes the absence portable and repeatable - a public image the person is not required to maintain for you, because the person died and the manufacture went on. It is filed under the shelf for the historic-as-character: the real woman flattened into a type the silkscreen imposes, and every accurate fact about her in tension with the attachment the picture invites.

nodes.t: Entitled to the adulation of all lesser mortals
nodes.s: A children's comic club that awarded membership badges, and whose membership card was authorised by a character.
nodes.g:
**The club exists so that a printed figure will appear to be writing to a child personally, and the child does the work.** Captain Marvel debuted on the cover of *Whiz Comics* #2, cover-dated February 1940, drawn by C. C. Beck from a script by Bill Parker under executive editor Wilford H. Fawcett - and the issue carried an offer: send in a code and receive a membership certificate, a membership card with your own code number, and a plastic Captain Marvel ring. The code was printed in the comic. **Every member had to decode the message themselves.** So the near side performed the decoding, and the impression of a secret channel was manufactured out of materials the far side printed. That is the part of this arrangement nobody writes about, and it is why this is an entry rather than a footnote to the Golden Age: **the parasocial bond was assembled by the person who was attached.**

**And the membership card was authorised by a character, which is the purest `simulated` reciprocity on this site.** The card's authorised wording reads: "Is a charter member in good standing of The Merry Marvel Marching Society And is thereby **entitled to the adulation and admiration of all lesser mortals!**" - and it was issued under "the actual authority of **Benj J. Grimm, Grand Marshal (pro tem)**". Grimm is the Thing. **The institution signed as a character**, so that a reply from a publisher would arrive with a fictional officer's signature on it and appear to come from inside the fiction rather than from a business. The card also declared that "these privileges are non-transferable", which is a reminder that the thing being sold was a status rather than an access.

**The adjacent clubs are the evidence that the signature was a choice.** Dell ran a comics club whose certificate was authorised by **G. T. Delacorte Jr.**, an actual person; Little Orphan Annie ran a code badge that in one account a boy waited anxiously for; E. C. began "to build a mailing list of fans willing to pay to belong to its fan club to get news of upcoming issues." **Four publishers, four devices, and the one that put a character in the signature is the one whose reply would read as coming from inside the story.** Nobody was deceived and nothing was fraudulent - the certificate said what it was - but a child holding a card signed by the Grand Marshal is holding something the adult in the shop never was.

**This is the first named instance of the `cog` register, and it satisfies all three conditions the register asks for at once.** The far end has its own machinery: this was a premium scheme, and "Bargain X" offered America's Greatest Comics #2, Gene Autry Comics #2, Minute Man Comics #3 and "a color picture of Spy Smasher for a quarter". Every member is one working part of a sales device aimed at their parents' pocket. And every member has their own machinery - the decoding. **None of the children built it, and the register's test is whether seeing the whole machine would change the attachment. It would not.** Seeing that the cipher was printed in the page does not make a reader stop being a reader. That is the register's whole content: "A cog that can see the machine is still a cog." Until this entry the register had a definition, a test and no instance, and a definition with nothing behind it prints on the taxonomy page as though it were a finding.

**The club was also promoted by a film, which closes the circle with this site's own argument.** The club was pushed by an actual feature, Frank Tashlin's *Good Humor Man* (1950), plus a Fawcett special issue - so a membership in a fictional boy's club was sold through a feature film, on a screen, to children who had never met the publishers who were writing to them.

**The commercial ending runs the other way from the usual story.** Marvel's fan clubs and their premiums "evolved, eventually culminating in a full-fledged kit for Wild Agents of Marvel **before being discarded as a potential profit center**." So the apparatus was retired because it did not pay - **the bond outlived the business plan, rather than the other way round**, which is the reverse of how parasocial attachment is usually written and is why the register exists.

**What the figures around it were worth.** *Whiz Comics* ran from February 1940 to June 1953, 155 issues, and Captain Marvel's sales "surpass[ed] that of DC stalwarts like Batman and Superman"; he was the first superhero to appear on film. Then **DC sued Fawcett in 1941 alleging the character violated its intellectual property, and the case took twelve years to resolve**, with Fawcett paying **$400,000** and ceasing publication of all Captain Marvel material, which ended the thirteen-year run. The far end of this tie was not merely silent or withdrawn; it was **legally removed**, and the club members had no say in it. That is the one hard fact in the entry that no club's own literature would tell you.

**A weakness in this entry's own sourcing, recorded rather than hidden.** The publication facts are solid and double-sourced - *Whiz Comics* #2's publisher, cover artist, writer and editor, the run dates, the lawsuit and the damages all come from Wikipedia and DC Database. **The artefacts - the certificate wording, the Grimm signature, the plastic ring, the decoding - rest on two weaker records**: a Comic-Con programme newsletter and a fan site that has recreated the code card. A club that awarded a plastic ring is exactly the sort of thing remembered differently by different people, which is why the wording above is quoted wherever a quote exists and paraphrased nowhere. If this entry is ever stood behind, the artefacts are the part to stand behind.

nodes.s: From 1962 Stan Lee ran fan mail in the back of The Fantastic Four and answered it in print in his own voice, so a reader could see their name answered on a page. The letters page became Marvel's institutional address to its readership, and its regular trophy, the No-Prize, was deliberately nothing.
nodes.g:
**The corpus keeps the datum that a reply used to be the exception. This is the same object with the exception removed.** From the early issues of The Fantastic Four, cover-dated 1962, Stan Lee printed readers' letters and answered them on the page. Lee's own 1992 account traces the habit to the Jerry Todd books, which printed readers' letters and the author's informal answers, and he concluded that "talking to the readers informally and indirectly seemed like the natural thing to do." The page ran polls - whether the Invisible Girl should leave the team - and offered five dollars for the best explanation of a continuity error.

The reply became a scheduled product. A contest whose prize was nothing got a name when its winner was announced, and the name stuck: the No-Prize. By the end of 1965 the letters section had grown into the house page, and from 1967 a regular column made the reply a fixture. The trophy became a posted ritual: winners were mailed a pre-printed empty envelope reading "this envelope contains a genuine Marvel Comics No-Prize which you have just won!", and some readers wrote back to ask where the prize had fallen out. **The award was the reply; the envelope was the receipt.**

The voice outlived the man: the page passed to the editors who followed Lee, which is the tell that the intimacy was institutional rather than personal. It belongs in this corpus where the intermediary that is also the relationship sits - the infrastructure for somebody else's attachment. A reader's name printed next to an answer is the demonstration of being seen while nothing on the other side was made available, and the demonstration was mass-produced on a schedule.

nodes.t: Known to more people than any other woman in history
nodes.s: The first film performer whose value could be counted instead of guessed. She was on the cover of the New York Dramatic Mirror in 1911, an honour then kept for theatrical stars; by 1916 her fan following had become ten thousand dollars a week, half her film profits and a production company of her own. The audience was never asked for any of it, and every line of the contract exists because of it.
nodes.g:
**The fan worship is in the contract.** St. John's line, as the American Experience page quotes it, is the scale the entry works from: Pickford was "known to more people and loved by more people than any other woman that has been in all history." Reach was the asset, and reach was countable. In 1911 she was the first movie star to adorn the cover of the New York Dramatic Mirror, an honour "previously bestowed only on theatrical stars" - the trade press had already decided that a moving-picture player could carry a cover, and the sentence that records it is careful to say what the honour used to be worth.

Then 1914 and Tess of the Storm Country. The record says the picture "caused a sensation", that it "created fan worship that had never before been witnessed", and that the success "gave Mary Pickford incredible bargaining power"; by 1916 she had "a $10,000 a week salary, 50% of her film profits, and her own production company." The chronology is kept rather than resolved: her foundation dates the renegotiation to May 1916, another account dates a contract at 24 June 1916 with a guarantee of $1.04 million. Both are here, because a date and a number that disagree are the ordinary state of a contract nobody was meant to read. United Artists followed in February 1919, with Fairbanks, Chaplin, Griffith and Hart.

The other side of it is why this is not a portrait. When the company she co-founded had its way, it would "pressure Pickford to limit herself artistically, playing roles she knew her fans would love." **Nobody voted and the studio obeyed anyway.** That is the shape of the whole period: an audience made sovereign and unaware of it, consulted through a contract clause rather than through a question. By 1927 the highs were over, and what the constraint had been buying was visible from the outside.

In turn, this success gave Mary Pickford incredible bargaining power. In 1916, Pickford had negotiated a contract that gave her a $10,000 a week salary, 50% of her film profits, and her own production company." nodes.s: Public mourning in a way that produced its own genre of documentary and speculation.
nodes.g: The moment grief for a parasocial figure became a media product, with outlets monetising speculation about the death itself. The line between honouring the dead and selling the death is drawn here, and it is not respected here.

src.citation: Grigsby Bates, K. (2009, June 25). Michael Jackson Dead At 50: The Two-Way. NPR.
src.claim: Fixes the date: Jackson died on Thursday 25 June 2009 at UCLA Medical Center, pronounced dead at 2:26pm, aged 50. Also documents the entry's actual subject from inside the first hours: TMZ reported the death first and CNN confirmed it more than two hours later via the Los Angeles coroner, and the publicist who had served Jackson during the 1991 molestation trial issued a statement to assembled reporters within the first night, describing him as 'impossibly difficult and often self-destructive'. Grief and access arriving as a media product, hours after the news, with no cooling-off period.

The full autopsy and toxicology reports were placed on security hold at the request of police and the district attorney, and federal and state agencies opened parallel investigations.

nodes.t: From two undelivered reels to a lunchbox
nodes.s: A cartoon mouse with a licensed lunchbox, a walk-of-fame star and a park where you can meet him - the first character to be manufactured as an object and then put back in the room with you.
nodes.g: This is `howdy-doody` nineteen years early and further along, and it is the point at which the fictional figure stops being a picture and becomes a product with a supply chain. Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks made him as a replacement for Oswald the Lucky Rabbit; he was "originally to be named 'Mortimer Mouse', until Disney's wife, **Lillian**, suggested 'Mickey'"; and his first two shorts, *Plane Crazy* and *The Gallopin' Gaucho*, **were not picked up for distribution**. The public debut was *Steamboat Willie* (1928) - the third attempt, and the one that worked, which is a useful reminder that the famous version is usually the version somebody retried. What makes the entry is the licensing. **"Since his early years, Mickey Mouse has been licensed by Disney to appear on many different kinds of merchandise. Mickey was produced as plush toys and figurines, and Mickey's image has graced almost everything from T-shirts to lunchboxes."** Over 130 films, a comic strip that ran 45 years, and a merchandising department run by **Kay Kamen from 1932 until his death in 1949**, "a 'stickler for quality'", named a Disney Legend in 1998 - which is the detail that matters, because the object pipeline needed somebody whose job was to police what the figure was allowed to appear on. The character was **licensed from the beginning**, which is the commercial form of `made`: the other end is worked by a company and sold back to you. And then the two facts that tie it to the rest of this corpus. In 1978 **Mickey became the first cartoon character to have a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame**, and he is described as **"a meetable character at the Disney parks"**. Meetable. A drawn figure who exists on a screen and cannot hear you became a person in a room who can see you - which is the whole of `the-fourth-wall`'s argument arriving fifty years early, and arriving as a ticket price.

src.citation: Mickey Mouse. Wikipedia.
src.claim: Origin and naming: 'The character was originally to be named "Mortimer Mouse", until Disney's wife, Lillian , suggested "Mickey". Mickey first appeared in two 1928 shorts Plane Crazy and The Gallopin' Gaucho (which were not picked up for distribution) before his public debut in Steamboat Willie (1928).' Creation: 'Mickey Mouse was created as a replacement for Oswald the Lucky Rabbit, an earlier cartoon character', by Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks. Reach: 'The character went on to appear in over 130 films, mostly short films... Since 1930, Mickey has been featured extensively in comic strips (including the Mickey Mouse comic strip, which ran for 45 years)'. And the pipeline: 'Since his early years, Mickey Mouse has been licensed by Disney to appear on many different kinds of merchandise. Mickey was produced as plush toys and figurines, and Mickey's image has graced almost everything from T-shirts to lunchboxes. Largely responsible for early Disney merchandising was Kay Kamen , Disney's head of merchandise and licensing from 1932 until his death in 1949, who was called a "stickler for quality".' Presence: 'he also appears in media such as video games as well as merchandising and is a meetable character at the Disney parks', and 'In 1978, Mickey became the first cartoon character to have a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.'

nodes.t: A mob is a parasocial event
nodes.s: Framing online harassment as a mob, and asking who is on it.
nodes.g: The most useful analytical frame available for a behaviour with no consequences for the people committing it, and the phrase that gets people to ask the question at all.

src.claim: THE PAPER'S OWN FRAMING IS THIS ENTRY. 'After an accusation of wrongdoing, an outrage mob appears. Initially, just a few condemn the accused. But before long, more and more people pile on, hastily meting out punishment with little regard for evidence or opposing perspectives.' Four studies, n=10,343
src.citation: Kteily, N., & Jordan, J. How reputation does (and does not) drive people to punish without looking.

src.claim: AND THE FINDING THAT CUTS AGAINST THE MORAL READING: there is NO reputational reward for not looking. Non-lookers were rated more loyal to the cause, but that was outweighed by a larger hit to perceived competence and fairness - evaluators rewarded punishers who LOOKED more generously
src.citation: Kteily & Jordan, How reputation does (and does not) drive people to punish without looking.

nodes.t: Thousands came to gawk at the empty wall
nodes.s: An Italian workman walked out of the Louvre with the painting under his coat, and the wall it had hung on went on drawing a crowd: four iron hooks, no picture, and thousands of people come to look at the hooks anyway. The papers printed the absence, and when she came back she had become public property - the first mass art icon, made by a thief rather than by a painter.
nodes.g:
**A crowd stood in front of an empty wall, and that is the whole entry.** The four hooks were still there and people came to look at them - "thousands of people came to gawk at the empty wall where the painting had once hung". L'Illustration printed the question the absence had raised for it: "What audacious criminal, what mystifier, what maniac collector, what insane lover, has committed this abduction?" A picture nobody could see was being discussed in the language reserved for a kidnapping, which is the correct language for the situation and is also the first time in this corpus that a crowd's attention is described as a taking rather than as a looking.

The scale is recorded twice and the two records do not agree. One has "more than 100,000 people viewed it" after the return; the other has "at least 120,000 people went to see the painting in the first two days after it was returned". Both are kept, because the disagreement is the evidence - numbers that size are what a public looks like once an object has become a story. The record also disagrees about the theft itself: one man, or three. That disagreement is kept too, and neither version changes a word of the entry, which is about the wall rather than about who carried her out of it.

What the theft produced is the sentence worth having. As the account the entry leans on puts it, "The Mona Lisa had left the Louvre a work of art. She returned as public property, the first mass art icon." Satirical postcards, a short film and cabaret songs followed, and "popular culture seized upon the theft and turned high art into mass art." **The image went on doing the work the canvas used to do, and the canvas came back as something people queued to be near.**

Peruggia is the one attachment in the record that answers itself. He said he had fallen "a victim to her smile" and feasted his eyes on his treasure every evening, which is a one-sided tie describing itself out loud and in a courtroom's vocabulary. The crowd had the same tie and no sentence for it, which is what the queue in front of the hooks was. **She was not there for either of them, and being not-there is the whole of the arrangement.**

nodes.s: Fifty-four years of letters to a fictional detective, answered by an office that had chosen not to have a face.
nodes.g:
The archive is the evidence here, not a metaphor. The New York Public Library's Stratemeyer Syndicate records hold the fan mail as a described subseries - boxes 56 and 57 - of "letters received from young readers of Syndicate books dating from 1930-1984", together with "a few letters written by parents on behalf of their children, and from adults who read Syndicate volumes during their childhood". **Fifty-four years, addressed to a girl who did not exist.** The finding aid's own summary is that "dozens of fan letters from young readers testify to the broad appeal of Syndicate publications". This is what an archive looks like when somebody simply keeps the letters of a tie that asked for nothing - which is why it is the only evidence such a tie ever produces.

**And there are recordings.** The same collection "includes commercial recordings of dramatic readings of Syndicate books, including stories from The Bobbsey Twins, Nancy Drew and Tom Swift. Also present are audio letters to Edna Stratemeyer Squier, and unidentified recordings." A child could send a voice and receive a voice in an era with no answering machine, and the reply was a physical object that has since been played to death. **The honest limit is on the entry: the finding aid does not record who those letters were addressed to, so this entry does not claim they were answers to children.** It claims that the company held audio letters and dramatic readings of Nancy Drew, which is what the document says.

**For the first forty-four years of that correspondence the readers were writing to somebody with no author.** The first Nancy Drew book appeared in April 1930 and Edward Stratemeyer died twelve days later. Mildred Wirt Benson wrote 23 of the first 30 books under the Syndicate-chosen house pseudonym **Carolyn Keene**, and that pseudonym was not a person - it was a slot in a production system, reused across series by writers who never met. **Benson's identity was not made public until 1991**, when staff and faculty at the University of Iowa established who Carolyn Keene had been. So for almost the whole life of the fan-mail subseries, every reply to a child's letter came from an office that had chosen not to have a face. The one detail on record about the series' quality comes from the same correspondence and is a marketing judgement: Stratemeyer thought Nancy Drew was "much too flip", and sent the manuscripts on anyway.

**The near side's own account was collected, which almost never happens.** The Carolyn Dyer papers at the Iowa Women's Archives hold materials from a 1993 Nancy Drew Conference including "testimonials from readers all over the country on what Nancy Drew meant to them", and *Rediscovering Nancy Drew* (University of Iowa Press, 1995) grew out of that meeting with a chapter titled "Reading the Stories of Reading: Nancy Drew Testimonials". **This site is an argument assembled from reader testimony, and here a hundred strangers wrote theirs down before anyone asked.**

**The register claim, and the motive it has to live with.** From the reader's side nothing was asked of the far end and nothing was paid, which is the `undemanded` test exactly - but the tie was *industrial* rather than unremarked. It had a business owner, a correspondence department, a house pseudonym and a schedule. So this is not the private case the register imagines; it is somebody noticing that children were writing and building the reply channel to meet them, which is the same decisive commercial move as a cereal company's decoder ring and considerably less cynical. What earns it the register is not that nobody profited - the Syndicate profited - but that the tie as the reader lived it asked for nothing and was answered anyway. **Wanting is the only part of a one-sided tie that is never anybody's fault**, and it is wanting that fifty-four years of letters is made of.

src.citation: New York Public Library, Stratemeyer Syndicate records, 1832-1984 (MssCol 2903) - finding aid
src.claim: The primary archival description, and the source of the entry's central claim. The Fan Mail subseries at boxes 56-57: "letters received from young readers of Syndicate books dating from 1930-1984. Also included are a few letters written by parents on behalf of their children, and from adults who read Syndicate volumes during their childhood." Also: "Dozens of fan letters from young readers testify to the broad appeal of Syndicate publications"; that the Syndicate "was established in 1905 by Edward Stratemeyer" as a book packaging company employing ghostwriters; that he "died in May of 1930, not long after the appearance of two of his most successful book series, The Hardy Boys and Nancy Drew"; that "commercial recordings of dramatic readings of Syndicate books, including stories from The Bobbsey Twins, Nancy Drew and Tom Swift" are in the collection along with "audio letters to Edna Stratemeyer Squier, and unidentified recordings"; and that Harriet Stratemeyer Adams revealed herself as the pseudonymous Carolyn Keene not long after Edna Squier's death in 1974. That last fact is recorded in RESEARCH-NOTES as NOT used for the authorship claim: Adams and Benson were different writers of the same pseudonym, and the 1991 Iowa finding is the one the entry relies on.

nodes.t: The dead kept in the cave
nodes.s: Neanderthals repeatedly carried their dead into one cave in northern Iraq and put them down in the floor. Shanidar 4 was found on his side with his arm under his head; Shanidar Z lay in a hollow gouged out to fit her, with a stone under her head. The cluster dates to roughly seventy to seventy-five thousand years ago.
nodes.g: The oldest evidence on this site of people treating the dead as somewhere you go, rather than something you leave behind. It sits about fifty-five thousand years before the dog, which settles an argument this site was getting wrong: one-sided attachment to a non-human does not begin with a domesticated animal. It is also the discipline case. The famous flowers were a mistake - the pollen turned out to come from burrowing rodents - and the burials survived the debunk anyway. That is what a real claim looks like after someone has been wrong about part of it. One limit worth stating: Sunghir, later and better studied, shows this was not a single uniform practice, so what Shanidar documents is the earliest *instance* of something that varied a great deal.

src.claim: Dates and method: repeated interment in the same cave; the most recent individual found in a shallow scoop partly covered by rocks that appear to have been placed, dated to around 70,000-75,000 years ago, with an earlier cluster at 70,000-60,000 and others at 45,000-50,000.
src.citation: University of Cambridge, Department of Archaeology. Shanidar Cave Project. Date of access recorded in tools/citation_audit_baseline.json run.

nodes.t: The finale that moved the schedule
nodes.s: A soap opera ends after decades and national broadcast schedules were rearranged around it.
nodes.g: Not an attachment to a character but to a piece of shared civic infrastructure, and grief measured academically in the same weeks. It is the clearest evidence that parasocial bonds can attach to a place, not a person.

nodes.s: The sculptor who fell in love with his own work. The statue was never going to be able to leave, and the story treats that as part of the appeal rather than a tragedy to be corrected.
nodes.g: Not the origin - the archaeology in this file runs tens of thousands of years further back, and Roman wax imagines predate Ovid by two and a half centuries. What this is: the first time the structure was written down deliberately, by a Roman, as a story worth telling about a man who loved something that could not leave. The telling detail was never that he loved a statue. It was that the statue was never going to be able to leave, and that this seems to have been part of the appeal. The feeling is real and entirely structured around the other party's inability to reciprocate, and everyone since has rediscovered it.

nodes.s: Paid message apps where a window shaped exactly like the one holding your best friend costs about four dollars a month per artist, plus anniversary counters that make the bond feel cumulative and streaks that convert it into a hostage situation.
nodes.g: The lane where the feeling is genuine and the design is not accidental. Every mechanism here was tested, found to work, and shipped. The person is not being scammed, which is exactly what makes it difficult - the affection is real and so is the invoice, and the industry is extremely good at keeping those two facts in separate mental drawers.

nodes.s: Upper Paleolithic carvers in Europe made small figures of animals and people from mammoth ivory from about forty thousand years ago. The Vogelherd set includes a cave lion, a bison, a horse, a bear, a mammoth, and a lion-man - a body with a human face on a lion's. At La Madeleine in France a bison carved from antler is caught mid-grooming, turning its head to lick its own side.
nodes.g: This is what the dog entry used to deny. Animals carrying human qualities were being made, kept and shown to other people tens of thousands of years before the dog: the grooming gesture is specifically human, and somebody carved it in antler on purpose. It also puts an anthropomorphised animal on the same taxonomy shelf as the dog roughly twenty-five thousand years ahead of it, which is the honest shape of the argument. The dog is not the first animal to be given human shape in the imagination. It is the first animal to be bred into living alongside us.

src.claim: Animal, human and hybrid figurines made by modern humans beginning at least 35,000 years ago, across a broad area of Europe, in a spread of sizes, shapes and styles made by different groups - including the Vogelherd cave lion, mammoth, bison and horse, and the lion-man.
src.citation: Smithsonian Institution, Human Origins Program. Figurines. Human Evolution Evidence: Behavior, Art & Music.

src.claim: The La Madeleine 'bison licking its side', Magdalenian, c. 14,000 years old, carved from the palmate section of a reindeer antler, shown turning to lick its own flank - a self-grooming gesture rendered in a portable object.

nodes.s: Whether a bond to somebody who does not know you exists can be a rights question at all.
nodes.g: The genuinely unsolved one. A relationship with no other party is not obviously covered by any consent framework, and the absence of a framework is where the harm goes. The elder-care analogy is the one that makes people uncomfortable and it is the one that fits.

nodes.s: A clinical name for a case where a one-sided bond is causing significant distress or impairment. Named in the eighties, and it is a real diagnosis for a small number of people.
nodes.g: The trouble is that the disorder and the ordinary bond are the same shape. The disorder requires distress - which means you cannot identify it from the strength of the feeling alone, only by asking what it is costing. That distinction is the whole point, and it is the one most coverage of the subject skips.

nodes.s: The name itself. Coined to describe the way viewers responded to a television character they followed consistently - a bond with somebody who did not know they existed. Parasocial: one-sided, parallel to the para- in paranormal.
nodes.g: The coinage is defensive and that is the story. It was invented in the McCarthy era to describe a television habit that was considered slightly shameful - viewers writing in about soap characters as though they could be defamed. The word bakes in an apology for the feeling. The feeling did not need one.

nodes.s: Using a one-sided bond to move somebody: the celebrity endorsement, the fan club vote, the ad that works because the viewer already feels known. And the finding that ads featuring attractive models can actively reduce purchase intention in people who feel excluded.
nodes.g: The double-edged result is the interesting part. The same mechanism that makes somebody buy the product can make them not buy it, purely as a function of whether they felt the ad was addressed to them. Persuasion runs through recognition, not through liking.

nodes.s: A season of a reality format and a global sporting event produce millions of viewers who then investigate the participants' personal lives. A relationship with an edited construct becomes a licence to intervene in a real life.
nodes.g: The whole mechanism in one summer: visibility mistaken for access, and access mistaken for entitlement. What the audience actually had was an eight-week window onto a version of a person that producers cut down to a confessional and got paid for. The gap between the two is invisible from inside the eight weeks.

nodes.t: Peak TV and the parasocial bargain
nodes.s: Prestige television as a sustained parasocial bargain: writers, actors and marketing presenting themselves as authors of a world viewers inhabit.
nodes.g: The high-water mark of the writer as parasocial object. Showrunners were discussed with the intimacy previously reserved for characters, and the parasocial frame explains the intensity better than any account of television as art does.

src.citation: Golden Age of Television (2000s-2023). Wikipedia.
src.claim: 'Peak TV' was not a critic's category or a scholarly one: it was coined by FX chief executive John Landgraf, and Wikipedia names him as such. Which matters, because the phrase was positioning - and the same entry records the corrective: streaming providers returned to releasing one episode a week in the early 2020s 'to address burnout from binge watching and concerns that the practice of releasing full seasons at once makes television more disposable and forgettable', with Landgraf among those worried the era had produced 'peak redundancy'. The schedule of the bond was being managed by the people selling it.

src.citation: Colman, E. (2024, April 1). Who Killed Prestige TV? Toward a 'Good Fan' Theory of Television. Literary Hub.
src.claim: A critic naming the mechanism in this site's terms: prestige TV 'draws its audience in to a Spotified relationship to art', offering 'personalization in lieu of experimentation', so that 'shows are shows. Niches are blockbusters are nichebusters. It's all television. This time with a faux-participatory aspect - a parasocial media.' Supports the entry's claim that showrunners and writers became parasocial objects, from the critical side.

nodes.t: The podcast as an intimate medium
nodes.s: A voice in your ear, unedited, twice a week, for years. The most parasocial habit in the English language and rarely discussed as such.
nodes.g: Nobody wears a costume and nobody mentions the format, so it never got examined. Researchers eventually measured it and found listeners score high on exactly the traits predicted: novelty-seeking, curiosity, and a need for good conversation.

nodes.s: A game event causes a physical stampede at a real stadium because players arrived to capture it in person.
nodes.g: A parasocial bond with software producing a crowd in a physical space, and the first time the parasocial frame had to explain a mass-casualty event rather than a feeling. Everyone in that stadium was a genuine participant, which is the difficulty.

No injuries are reported here. Corrects the entry's location and its implied casualty toll.

src.citation: Associated Press (2016, July 10). Getting hurt, mugged and even finding a dead body with Pokemon Go. CBC News.
src.claim: The actual 2016 harm, which was a scatter of individual incidents rather than a mass-casualty event: a skateboard crash, players entering a Darwin police station because it was a PokeStop, an armed robbery police in Missouri said the game may have prompted, and players who were in fact meeting face to face. This is what the record supports: real individual harm and a lot of unexpected sociability, not a stampede.

src.claim: The stadium-scale crowd event, a year later than the entry's date and in a park rather than a stadium: the inaugural Pokemon GO Fest in Chicago's Grant Park, where server and authentication failures produced repeated surges at the main stage, a chant of 'Fix the servers', booing of the onstage host and of Niantic's CEO, and players leaving en masse. A crowd physically organised by a game mechanic, and a refusal to leave. Not a crush.

nodes.s: A costume is put on by a new actor and the audience transfers its entire attachment to whoever is now inside it. Running five days a week, in front of millions of children, with nobody pretending otherwise.
nodes.g: The most complete parasocial handover ever broadcast, and the closest thing television has to a controlled experiment. The audience knew the person had changed. They transferred the feeling anyway, instantly, and enjoyed knowing they were doing it.

nodes.g: Grief engineered to announce itself, and the parasocial bond used deliberately as a broadcast channel by the person who had it.

nodes.g: A technical innovation that produced a psychological one. Putting the camera inside somebody's eyes makes the audience's position structurally identical to the character's, which is the whole friendship with a film in one device.

nodes.s: The only intervention on this site that you do to yourself, and the only one nobody else can do for you. List your five strongest one-sided ties, score joy and cost, keep three, mute one, trade one hour a week toward a person in the room.
nodes.g: Not a cure and not a diagnostic. A rebalancing, done badly, about four times a year. It exists because the seventh law is the only part of the field that is actually yours, and because the numbers - one to ten, twice - make a feeling arguable.

nodes.s: A woman's misfortune told aloud, a crowd's reaction converted into a number, and the number chose her.
nodes.g:
**A machine returned the verdict on somebody's life.** The format that actually broadcast is not the one most people remember. The host interviewed four or five women one at a time, each telling her personal troubles - a terminally sick child at home, a disabled husband out of work, the need for a hearing aid, a washing machine, a refrigerator - and then **the audience chose the winner by applauding**. The source is exact about the instrument: she "who received the greatest amount of applause **as registered by the 'applause meter'** was Queen for a Day." So a woman's hardship was narrated aloud, a room's reaction was converted into a reading, and the reading decided. **Every other `cog` case in this corpus argues the point structurally; this one has a box on a wall with a needle in it.** The register asks whether seeing the whole machine changes the attachment - and here the machine is not a metaphor for a set of relations, it is the thing that did the choosing.

**And the instrument was pointed at the wrong room, which is the honesty note that makes it sharper rather than weaker.** In radio the home listener could not participate at all. The crowd the meter registered was the **studio** audience - as the format has it, the audience was asked "Would you like to be Queen for a Day?", "YES!!!!" shouted the audience, and "the audience cheered to pick their favorite one" - while the millions listening at home could not applaud into the device. **So the applause meter was not a proxy for the audience's feeling. It measured a different and much smaller audience than the one listening.** The far end was not merely unseen; its measuring instrument was aimed elsewhere. That is a sharper claim than "the audience picked the winner", and it is the one the sources support.

**The prize was a fictional figure assembled out of a real woman's misfortune.** The prize list is a Cinderella transformation in full: "It starred their friends and neighbors, and **turned them into fabulous Cinderellas** with such prizes as a charming five-star luncheon with a friend, a roll down the red carpet at a movie studio, a beauty analysis, Hollywood makeup and hairdo, escort through the Boulevard, dining on the finest steaks and tropical fruits, then dancing at the finest star-studded clubs." **The object of the public's attachment is a Queen, and she is built weekly out of a neighbour's hardship** - one contestant asked for "an operation for her sick cat". So the parasocial figure is manufactured from real grief, and the grief is then explained as a commercial. Jack Bailey's sign-off is the thesis of the format in eight words: **"Make every woman a queen, for every single day!"**

**And the throne was where the performance was compulsory.** Documented as mood dissonance: after being crowned, the contestant "was expected to sit on a throne and listen to a five minute in-show commercial about all the consumer items that she'd just won, **while pretending to be really excited and thankful about the benefits of things like aluminum cookware and dog treats**." **A woman who has just asked in public for surgery for her child is then required to perform gratitude to a sponsor, on air, for five minutes.** That is `simulated` reciprocity aimed at the person being pitied rather than at the audience, and it is the most uncomfortable mechanism in this corpus - because the performance is compulsory and the person performing it has the least power in the room to refuse it. The audience's attachment is real; the contestant's half of it is a sponsorship read.

**The sorrow slot was sold by the minute.** Sponsored by Malted Milk, and the network's own arithmetic is the record: the show was so popular that the network extended it from 30 to 45 minutes "so they could sell more commercial time at the then astounding rate of **$4000 per minute**". So the position of the contestant with the worst story was worth money to somebody, and the schedule is the receipt.

**The shape of the thing, briefly, because it is genuinely a forerunner and the corpus should say so on its own terms.** Created by John Masterson, debuting on the Mutual network on **30 April 1945** as *Queen for Today*, hosted first by Ken Murray; a few months in it moved to Los Angeles, took the name *Queen for a Day*, and Jack Bailey - a former vaudeville musician and World's Fair barker - took over, simulcasting on television from 1948 through a DuMont affiliate whose owner also owned Mutual's Los Angeles radio station. Radio ran to 1957; it went to NBC television in 1956 and ABC in 1960. **The transition that made the device possible is in its own dates**: the applause meter needs a room, and the room arrived on schedule alongside the contest.

**Two honesty notes on this entry's own sourcing**, because the weakest records are also the most load-bearing. The applause-meter wording - the entry's title and its central claim - comes from Simple English Wikipedia, which is a wiki and should be stood behind. The throne behaviour and the mood-dissonance description come from TV Tropes, which is user-edited and is the weakest source here. The $4000-per-minute figure comes from a fan site and is **not** corroborated anywhere in what was read, so it is the first thing to check. The publication and format facts - creator, host, dates, networks, prizes, running time - are corroborated across the Television Academy's own archive and two independent catalogues, and those can be relied on.

These troubles might involve a terminally sick child at home, a husband disabled and out of work, or the need for a hearing aid or a new washing machine"; that **"The audience chose the winner by applauding their favorite. She who received the greatest amount of applause as registered by the 'applause meter' was Queen for a Day"**; that the winner "was crowned, escorted by attendants to a throne, and given not only what she wanted, but juicy prizes like high-end appliances, upscale fashions, and exotic vacation trips as well"; that the show launched on radio on 30 April 1945 and ran there until 1957, then NBC television 1956 to 1964; that "The program is something of an early 'reality show'"; and that "the show was so popular that NBC increased its running time from 30 minutes to 45 minutes." **A wiki, and the load-bearing claim for the title - the first thing to stand behind.**
