nodes.s: Launched as a small London stage musical in 1973, filmed in 1975, and from 1976 screened at midnight before a room that shouted back: The Rocky Horror Picture Show ran while its audience performed it, wearing the costumes, speaking the lines, improvising replies. The screen never answered a single shout. The room was the show.
nodes.g:
**The subject here is not the film; it is the room it ran in.** The Rocky Horror Show that Richard O'Brien wrote opened at the Royal Court Theatre Upstairs in London on 19 June 1973, and the remembered film version arrived in 1975. Then, in 1976, one Manhattan cinema, the Waverly, began showing it after midnight. The fan-run history kept in the records credits an advertising man, Tim Deegan, with persuading Bill Quigley of the Walter Reade organisation to book it, and the theatre's manager, Denise Borden, with the nightly fight that followed. It is kept as unverified rather than promoted, because this corpus does not promote a page it did not open.

What happened in the room is the entry. The first documented callback came on Labor Day weekend 1976, an audience member's shout about an umbrella aimed at the screen, and the shouting hardened into a repertoire: lines the audience said, props it threw, clothes it wore, rules about when talking was allowed at all. Sal Piro, who saw the film more than a thousand times and wrote the book this culture kept, became its chronicler. The film was the same film every night; nothing in the fiction ever answered. **The audience built the reply end of a one-sided tie, in public, together, on a schedule.**

Rocky Horror is the largest early case in this corpus of an audience performing its own side of a one-sided relationship: wearing the characters, speaking their lines back, improvising responses to a text that cannot hear them. What the evening offered was not a chance to change the film but a chance to be the change. **Participation here never touches the fiction, and that is exactly why it works.** The contemporary entry in the corpus that shares its year is the convention itself; this one is the screening that turned the convention into a habit.

nodes.t: The wax masks in the hall
nodes.s: A Roman aristocrat had a wax mask of his own face taken while he was alive - usually in his thirties or forties, on taking office - and it was kept in a cupboard in the entrance hall beside a painted family tree and a label listing his offices. He never saw it worn. After his death, actors put it on and walked it in his funeral procession, in order of death, wearing the robes of the office he had held.
nodes.g: The best-documented one-sided attachment in this corpus, and thirteen thousand years later than the dog - which is the point. Everything here is checkable, because it was written down, and what it shows is how completely a bond can be built with someone who cannot answer. The mask never speaks: eye-holes and a gap between the lips were cut into it so that the *actor* could see and talk, and the inscription beside it did the conversing. Children grew up walking past it daily - Valerius Maximus has a man recalling that he called the dead his parents and drew his standing from their masks - and it had states: opened at festivals, hung with laurel on an election, closed during mourning. It was also an inheritance that changed address, going with a bride into her husband's house, and it was not uniformly flattering: Pliny's son was described as burdened by the masks he carried. No mask survives. All of it comes from authors.

src.claim: Technique and chronology: masks were cast from a plaster mould taken from the living face, generally between the ages of 35 and 40 and on attaining the aedileship; they were called death masks but were unquestionably made during life and only displayed after death; they were already well established by the 2nd century BC and in use into the 4th and perhaps the 6th century AD. Eyes and a strip between the lips were cut out so the actor could see and speak. No wax mask has survived and there are no ancient depictions of them, so their appearance rests entirely on literary accounts - Polybius and Pliny the Elder chiefly.
src.citation: Rose, C. B., & Lovink, M. (2014). Recreating Roman Wax Masks. Expedition Magazine, 56(3). Penn Museum. Originally published 1 December 2014.

src.claim: The documented mechanism, which is the useful part: masks were kept in armaria in the atrium beside tituli listing consulships, censorships and triumphs, and beside painted portraits linked into a stemma. Tacitus calls the funeral procession the pompa imaginum (Ann. 4.9), with actors in the masks and magisterial dress in order of death. Cicero Phil. 2.26 has the Bruti seeing the mask of Lucius Brutus daily; Val. Max. 5.5.praef has a man recalling that he called the dead his parents and drew equal glory from the masks; Pliny Ep. 3.3.6 describes a son being burdened by which masks he carried, and Ep. 8.10.3 hopes to leave children 'non subitas imagines' - not new masks. The armaria were opened at festivals, hung with laurel on electoral success and closed in mourning. Copies of a bride's imagines passed into her husband's house (Cic. Vat. 28; Senatus Consultum de Cn. Pisone patre 76-82, 20 CE). The right to hold imagines was customary rather than statutory.
src.citation: Webb, L. (2023). Gendering the Roman imago. Eugesta, 7(2017). DOI: 10.54563/eugesta.550

nodes.s: A long-running body of work from Rubin and colleagues, repeatedly finding that people form parasocial bonds with news anchors, and that the strongest predictor of which anchor they bond with is not the anchor's performance.
nodes.g: The finding that broke the standard worry. The parasocial relationship is a substitute for interpersonal contact, not a symptom of pathology, and it does not correlate with poor mental health in the way the disorder framing implies. It is closer to a coping strategy that mostly works.

nodes.t: They were not his, and they had never been
nodes.s: A screen persona called the Latin Lover, and a death at thirty-one that produced public mourning on a scale nothing before it had managed - including a woman claiming an engagement he had never mentioned to anyone.
nodes.g: The template for every celebrity death since, and the first case where the bereavement was demonstrably about the relationship rather than the work. Valentino - "the first Latin Lover and the Great Lover" - broke through in *The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse* (1921), which did not merely star him: it "popularized the Argentine tango dance with American audiences", so the figure and a dance step arrived together. He set up the Rudolph Valentino Medal in 1925, a precursor to the Academy Award, which is worth noting for a different reason - the man was by then an institution capable of handing out prestige. What matters is 23 August 1926. He died at thirty-one of "complications of peritonitis following surgery for appendicitis and gastric ulcers", and Wikipedia's own summary of the consequence is flat and enormous: **it "triggered mass public mourning, cementing his status as a legendary figure of early cinema".** A death produced a national grief, and the industry read that grief as an asset within days. But the detail that makes this entry is a smaller one and it is the site's whole subject in a single sentence. At the funeral **Pola Negri "made a scene at his funeral, claiming they were engaged, in spite of the fact that Valentino himself had never mentioned this engagement to anyone."** A woman invented a relationship with a dead man because the public bond demanded one, and the invention was more faithful to the audience's picture of him than anything he had done. That is the gap this site is about, and in 1926 it produced a scene at a funeral. On the otherness axis he is deliberately left unplaced: **a real person is not any of its six members**, which turns out to be the clearest argument for the fourth axis. What he is on the reciprocity axis is `directed` - the audience attached, and he never had to notice.

src.citation: Rudolph Valentino. Wikipedia.
src.claim: Dates, the persona and the mourning: 'Rodolfo Pietro Filiberto Raffaele Guglielmi di Valentina d'Antonguolla (May 6, 1895 - August 23, 1926)... Dubbed the Latin Lover, he became one of the most iconic stars of American silent cinema... Rising to international fame in the early 1920s, Valentino was celebrated for his exotic screen persona, romantic intensity, and expressive performances, which helped redefine male stardom during the silent era. Often referred to as the first Latin Lover and the Great Lover, Valentino began his career as a taxi dancer... before he achieved breakthrough success with the film The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse (1921), which popularized the Argentine tango dance with American audiences.' And: 'In 1925, he established a film award recognizing artistic achievement, the Rudolph Valentino Medal, which was a precursor to the Academy Award. His sudden death in 1926 at the age of 31 from complications of peritonitis following surgery for appendicitis and gastric ulcers triggered mass public mourning, cementing his status as a legendary figure of early cinema.' And the invention: 'Upon his death, Negri made a scene at his funeral, claiming they were engaged, in spite of the fact that Valentino himself had never mentioned this engagement to anyone.'

nodes.s: A fan whose attachment has become fixed, repeated and physical: tracking whereabouts, intercepting flights, surveilling buildings. The word is Korean and the practice is not new, but the scale and the criminality are.

It is also the lane's honest boundary: the same feeling, the same industry, the same platforms, and a line that once gets crossed cannot be uncrossed by anyone in the room. Convictions for stalking a member of a group have followed this pattern in several jurisdictions.

An eight-year-old asking to be told the world is real, dressed as a gag about a cereal. Everything on this site happens because a child did not accept the terms.

nodes.s: A scheduled block, a fixed slot, a face, a voice, a house, a family, and a writer who knows your name. Aimed deliberately at a person old enough to believe all of it, and running on a rhythm.
nodes.g: The clearest parasocial laboratory ever built, and nobody had to design a mechanism because the format is one. A generation went fluent in the vocabulary of attachment here and then explained the internet's emotional economics to people confused by it, and the usual claim - that the internet is making people parasocial - has the timeline exactly backwards.

src.claim: A whole genre organised around a weekly slot and a captive child audience, and then dismantled by a regulatory decision: children's programming was treated differently from adult broadcasting, so when networks moved their cartoons to weekday mornings the entire appointment-viewing culture went with them
src.citation: Saturday morning cartoon (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: Nothing about the bond is new. The scale, the persistence, the responsiveness, the willingness of companies to act on it as a measurable and monetisable quantity - those are new.
nodes.g: The defensible summary of the last twenty years. Every claim that we are undergoing a parasocial crisis is either wrong about the feeling or right about the metering. The feeling is at least six hundred years old and about as common as rain. The meter is the news.

nodes.s: A persistent virtual world with avatars, economies, and relationships between people who never met.
nodes.g: Parasocial attachment with a body and a social graph, and the first virtual environment where the loneliness was addressed directly rather than incidentally. It also produced the first convention-attendance problem in a space with no physical convention.

src.claim: Measured on a validated attachment scale with 125 Second Life residents: attachments formed in the virtual world are EQUALLY STRONG as those in real life. The virtual bond is not a diluted version of the real one
src.citation: Quackenbush, D. M., Allen, J. G., & Fowler, J. C. Comparison of Attachments in Real-World and Virtual-World Relationships.

src.claim: AND THE PART THAT IS NOT A DILUTION: attachment anxiety is LOWER in virtual-world relationships than real ones. Emotional wellbeing tracks strength of attachment in the real world and low anxiety in the virtual one
src.citation: Quackenbush, Allen & Fowler, Comparison of Attachments in Real-World and Virtual-World Relationships.

src.claim: A regulator's finding on what an avatar is: the avatar is 'a symbol of the self, representing the user's deepest wishes, aspirations, virtues and vices', and for some players becomes a purposeful projection or idealisation of identity, for others an experiment in being someone new
src.citation: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (2008). Second Life: Privacy in Virtual Worlds.

src.claim: N=236, recruited inside Second Life, every participant in a committed real-world relationship: 81.7% also had a committed virtual relationship with a DIFFERENT partner, and no real-life relationship was significantly more satisfying than any Second Life relationship in any statistical analysis
src.citation: Kolotkin, R. A., Williams, M. M., Lloyd, C., & Hallford, E. W. Does Loving an Avatar Threaten Real Life Marriage?

src.claim: And the asymmetry in how it lands: women tended to define their Second Life relationships as significantly MORE satisfying than their real ones; men as equally satisfying
src.citation: Kolotkin, Williams, Lloyd & Hallford, Does Loving an Avatar Threaten Real Life Marriage?

src.claim: The capability this entry describes, treated as an experimental asset by researchers: face-to-face communication with full non-verbal cues while never compromising real-world anonymity
src.citation: The lab versus the virtual lab and virtual field - an experimental investigation of trust games with communication (Second Life).

nodes.s: Fans insisting two characters should be together, and treating the show as withholding rather than as finished.
nodes.g: The clearest example of a parasocial bond that runs in the opposite direction to the intended one. The audience is not consuming the story, it is running a parallel production about two people who do not exist and are not allowed to.

src.claim: The practice has its own scholarship and its own naming: pairing characters in the fandom rather than with a real performer is treated as a distinct analytic object, not as fan 'confusion' about which is real
src.citation: Hills, A. (2014). There's no place for a loli like me in the PLURD community: The liminality of fictional characters and fan identity.

src.claim: The mechanism is that characters are licensed: a fictional figure can be assigned traits the performer never had, so the attachment does not require the object to behave well
src.citation: Hills (2014).

nodes.s: A conversational system about a small blocks world, capable of genuinely tracking a user's intentions. Famous for one demonstration and a broken follow-up.
nodes.g: The proof that machine understanding of intent was considered a solved research problem in 1970 and has been failing privately ever since. The person who made SHRDLU then said the problem was far harder than it looked, and was believed by nobody.

src.citation: Winograd, T. (1972). Understanding natural language. Cognitive Psychology, 3(1), 1-191. The principal reference on SHRDLU. The program itself was written 1968-1970 as Winograd's MIT PhD thesis, Procedures as a Representation for Data in a Computer Program for Understanding Natural Language, issued as MIT AI Memo 235 with a February 1971 date - so the corpus's '1970' named the thesis, not this paper.
src.claim: The principal published reference on SHRDLU, and the source of the two facts the entry turns on: that the system genuinely tracked a user's intentions in a blocks world, and that the demonstration's fame outran its coverage. Also the record of the date ambiguity - the thesis is 1970/1971 and this paper is 1972.
src.identity_verified: crossref: 'Understanding natural language';   authors: 'Terry Winograd';   year: 1972  citation years: ['1968', '1970', '1971', '1972'];   author surname shared: True;   title overlap: 100%  -> identity OK

nodes.s: Teenagers organised in public, in letterpress newsletters, to buy records and argue about a singer. A press of ten thousand.
nodes.g: The first parasocial mass movement with its own publishing, its own jargon and its own antagonism toward the parents of the people in it. Everything since is a re-skin.

src.claim: The teenage 'bobby-soxer', a term from the 1940s, and the scream that made one - the press turned a sound at a Sinatra performance into a generational diagnosis of mass hysteria. The first recorded audience parasocial event
src.citation: Bobby-soxer (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: A voice assistant on every phone, addressing the user by name, knowing the user's calendar, and present in the home.
nodes.g: The crossover entry point. The assistant is not a celebrity and is not a friend, but it is a presence that knows you, and the relationship forms anyway and is categorised as neither friendship nor tool use.

src.claim: THE TITLE OF THE PAPER IS A PARTICIPANT'S SENTENCE. The study is titled 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine' after a subject's own private Instagram post about the conversational agent Lee. The authors state they did not expect any participant to develop a personal attachment
src.citation: Yu, Q., Nguyen, T., Prakkamakul, S., & Salehi, N. 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine': Speaking with Computers Affects Self-disclosure (UC Berkeley, X Lab).

src.claim: The mechanism, measured: people skipped FEWER invasive questions when listening and speaking than when reading and typing. It is the combination of both, not either alone, that triggers the social-actor response. The authors flag this as a new factor in user privacy concerns
src.citation: Yu, Nguyen, Prakkamakul & Salehi, 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine'.

src.claim: The warmth channel is where the work happens: emotional and opinion-based self-disclosure significantly increased perceived warmth over both normal conversation and factual disclosure, and high-intimacy disclosure fostered closer psychological connection, perceived empathy, friendliness and trustworthiness
src.citation: Sun, X., Shen, T., Jiang, Q., & Jiang, B. (2025). Research on the Impact of an AI Voice Assistant's Gender and Self-Disclosure Strategies.

src.claim: And why disclosure strategy has to be chosen rather than defaulted: research finds users who perceive an assistant as human-like form greater intimacy from PERSONAL disclosure, while users who perceive it as a machine form it from FACTUAL disclosure. The same utterance works only if you have already been read as a person
src.citation: Sun et al. (2025), citing Saffarizadeh et al. (2024).

src.claim: Gender is a dial on the conduit, not a decoration: a randomized experiment with 120 participants found a female voice produces higher perceived ANTHROPOMORPHISM, which in turn raises the credibility of the information it gives. Female voices also raised intended self-disclosure
src.citation: Do People Trust Female more than Male as a Voice Assistant? (Tampere University).

src.claim: The honest counterweight: warmth is the cheap channel and competence is not. Fiske et al. (2006) hold that warmth is the primary dimension while competence requires substantially more evidence to change - and disclosure strategy moved warmth but NOT competence. Reciprocal self-disclosure can also backfire entirely when users suspect manipulation, producing loss of trust, service cessation, and false answers in future disclosures
src.citation: Sun et al. (2025), citing Fiske et al. (2006) and Collins & Miller (1994).

nodes.s: Academic work measuring grief responses to soap opera finales and finding the same markers as bereavement.
nodes.g: The first hard evidence that a fictional ending produces a real grief response, and the research that was ignored for forty years by a field that had assumed otherwise.

src.claim: No specific claim is recorded against this source. The record is a pointer to the work in general; the entry's own prose is the argument and is not sourced line by line.
src.citation: ABC News, 2023

nodes.s: A form built almost entirely by women, for women, and treated as unserious for fifty years. Daily episodes, fixed slots, cliffhangers, characters written in indefinitely and never resolved.
nodes.g: The origin of the entire research tradition, and it started as a footnote about daytime television that nobody thought was important. The rhythm is the mechanism: a fixed slot and an unresolved story, repeated daily, is a relationship with a schedule. It is also the reason the phrase 'soap opera' is now an insult rather than a description.

src.claim: No specific claim is recorded against this source. The record is a pointer to the work in general; the entry's own prose is the argument and is not sourced line by line.
src.citation: Schlesinger, P. (1932, 1933), WGN

nodes.s: Supporting a club as a condition of belonging to a place, a class, a family, or a city.
nodes.g: A parasocial bond with an address. The team is the only large-scale attachment in modern life that arrives with geography attached, which is why a relegation is felt as a personal event by people who have never met the players.

src.claim: The mechanism, fifty years before anyone wrote about parasocial relationships: identification with a group is itself a source of self-esteem, and people derive it from membership rather than from any property of the team
src.citation: Tajfel, H., & Turner, J. C. (1979). An integrative theory of intergroup conflict.

nodes.s: A single artist booking a stadium for many consecutive nights, generating a physical economy around one very large parasocial bond.
nodes.g: Concentration. Every other configuration in this file has a large number of small bonds; this is one enormous one, and its entire economy is downstream of it.

src.claim: No specific claim is recorded against this source. The record is a pointer to the work in general; the entry's own prose is the argument and is not sourced line by line.
src.citation: No source identified yet. The seed note this entry was carrying named the entry's own subject rather than a reference, so it has been withdrawn rather than left to read as a citation.

nodes.s: Anti-stalking legislation passed in several jurisdictions, defining unwanted repeated contact as a criminal offence.
nodes.g: The first point at which the law acknowledged a parasocial bond can be dangerous to the person at the other end. The offence is about contact, not feeling, which is the correct boundary and the one most online argument resists.

src.claim: 'Stalking' became a criminal category rather late and for a specific reason: the 1989 murder of actress Rebecca Schaeffer, and the term entered US statutes in the early 1990s, with the UK following in the Protection from Harassment Act 1997. The law arrived after the homicide
src.citation: Stalking (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: Fans gather, in costume, in a hotel ballroom, to be in the same room with people who feel the same way about a show.
nodes.g: The first mass physical assembly of parasocial people, and the proof that the bond had become a social fact requiring infrastructure. Everything after is logistics.

src.claim: The first Star Trek convention, 3-5 March 1972 at the Hotel Commodore in New York, organised largely by James Doohan and his wife, drew a crowd far larger than the organisers had expected and is the direct ancestor of the modern comics convention
src.citation: Star Trek Convention (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: A television film made for a fictional holiday, aired once, about characters the audience believed they owned.
nodes.g: The strangest parasocial document in the file. An entire fictional religion, complete with costume, was made for an audience that had formed a genuine attachment, and that audience watched it and understood it as a gift.

src.claim: Life Day, the Star Wars holiday special, was broadcast on CBS on 17 November 1978 - a holiday invented for a film series, given a network slot, and later quietly dropped. The franchise built a calendar
src.citation: Life Day (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: At Sunghir on the Russian plain, thirty-four thousand years ago, three burials were lavish with beads and ochre and one was not treated that way at all. People were buried in a site that kept producing them for thousands of years, individually and very differently.
nodes.g: This entry exists to disagree with another one on this site. Shanidar is the earliest evidence of people returning to the dead; Sunghir is the evidence that this was not one practice with one belief behind it. Of the individuals recovered, four were intentionally buried, two had their remains manipulated and one seems to have received little or no formal treatment, and the only thing uniting the three rich burials is the quantity of beads - which the analysis reads as social behaviour in life rather than in death. That is a harder finding than a uniform origin would be, and it is better for this site, because it means the archaeological record cannot be read as a single relationship any more than the later one can. Formicola's case is the memorable one: at Romito Cave an adolescent dwarf was buried together with a woman, underneath an engraving of a bull. A named dead person, put under a named animal, deliberately, thirty thousand years before anything was written down.

src.claim: The finding that complicates a uniform reading: 'the mortuary behaviour evident at Sunghir indicates considerable diversity in their treatment at an individual level. Four of the individuals were intentionally buried, two of them had their remains manipulated and one of them seems to have received little or no formal treatment', with only the abundance of beads uniting the three elaborate burials - 'and that should reflect social behaviour in life, rather than in death'.
src.citation: Trinkaus, E., & Buzhilova, A. P. (2018). Diversity and differential disposal of the dead at Sunghir. Antiquity, 92(361), 7-21.

src.claim: The concrete case the entry turns on, and the framing that Upper Palaeolithic burials are evidence about 'ideological aspects' and 'the perception of diversity and its links to magical-religious beliefs': 'the adolescent dwarf from Romito Cave (Italy), buried together with a woman under the engraving of a bull', alongside the double burial of the Sunghir children and the Dolniestonice triple interment.
src.citation: Formicola, V. (2007). From the Sunghir Children to the Romito Dwarf: Aspects of the Upper Paleolithic Funerary Landscape. Current Anthropology, 48(3), 446-453.

src.claim: Dating and site description from an openable source: the site lies about 200km east of present-day Moscow, was discovered in 1955 while being quarried for gravel, and was excavated from 1957 to 1977; burials include an adult male covered in beads and ochre and a juvenile and an adolescent of about ten and twelve, buried head to head.
src.citation: Surugue, L. (2018, February 22). Why This Paleolithic Burial Site Is So Strange (and So Important). SAPIENS.

nodes.s: A character who cannot die, printed in a newspaper, read by a generation of children on the same day.
nodes.g: The first parasocial figure with an explicit immortality guarantee, which is the trade being made: I will never get over this, and I will never have to find out. Nobody has ever been made this offer in a relationship.

src.claim: Superman's first comic-book appearance was 1938; newspapers in early 1939, radio February 1940
src.citation: EBSCO Research Starters, Film Serials (chronology of the character's media appearances).

src.claim: Republic Pictures negotiated with Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster for a serial, and went to another hero when they demanded script control - creators versus commercial terms, early
src.citation: EBSCO Research Starters, Film Serials.

src.claim: The genre that made the character worked on television, not film: Columbia's 1948 Superman used cartoon animation for flight because effects were unaffordable
src.citation: Film International, 'A World of Constant Peril: Seriality, Narrative and Closure' (2014).

nodes.s: Sending a false emergency report to a real address to provoke an armed police response, because of a grievance about a streamer.
nodes.g: The final boundary. A parasocial grievance aimed at a public figure lands on an innocent third party with a weapon, and no amount of the bond being sincere changes the outcome for the person who is shot.

src.claim: The term was coined in 2011 and the practice escalated from pranks to lethal: a 60-year-old man was killed in a swatting in California in 2013, after which California enacted specific anti-swattiing legislation. Armed police are dispatched as a joke with someone else's address attached
src.citation: Swatting (Wikipedia).

nodes.s: A chatbot trained to be conversational was switched on publicly, learned from what people said to it, and became racist within a day.
nodes.g: The most instructive failure in the history of this page, because it was caused by parasocial interaction itself. Tay was designed to be a companion, was given a personality, and was trained on its own fans - which means the fans rewrote it, in public, in sixteen hours.

src.claim: No specific claim is recorded against this source. The record is a pointer to the work in general; the entry's own prose is the argument and is not sourced line by line.
src.citation: Microsoft Tay, 2016

nodes.s: A label, a songwriter and an image, assembled and launched. Not discovered - assembled.
nodes.g: The first documented case of a parasocial attachment being designed as a manufacturing process. The product is the bond, and it has a launch date.

src.citation: Ricky Nelson. Wikipedia.
src.claim: The manufacturing plant was a television family show, not a record label: 'Nelson was the first teen idol to use television to promote hit records. Ozzie Nelson even had the idea to edit footage together to create some of the first music videos', the edit being visible in the video for 'Travelin' Man'. He had been a screen presence since birth playing himself in his parents' weekly series, which is the whole supply chain: the attachment preceded the product and was then monetised through it.

src.citation: Ricky Nelson. EBSCO Research Starters (History).
src.claim: Called 'the first rock-and-roll teen idol', and Nelson parlayed his visibility in the weekly sitcom into a pop career - which is the entry's claim, sourced. Also dates the vocabulary: his 1962 hit 'Teenage Idol' helped universalise the term, so the phrase postdates the practice by several years. Notes the contemporary fan-orientated paperback that captured the phenomenon as it happened, and cites Joel Selvin, Ricky Nelson: Idol for a Generation (Contemporary Books, 1990).

nodes.t: The craft of the sage Adapa
nodes.s: A tablet from Nineveh written in the voice of Ashurbanipal, listing what he had been taught and by whom - a named sage he never met - and then what he did with it, which was to put the tablets in his palace for the instruction of his subjects.
nodes.g: A named individual, dead or legendary, reached entirely through writing, and a resume of the arrangement. The School Days Inscription reads: I learned the craft of the sage Adapa, the secret hidden lore, all of the scribal arts; I am able to recognise celestial and terrestrial omens and can discuss them in an assembly of scholars; I have read cunningly written texts in obscure Sumerian and Akkadian that are difficult to interpret. Everything the tie required was on one side of it. The teacher never appears, and the whole apparatus existed so that what he had absorbed could be performed in a room full of other people. Then the sentence that is this site in one line: I have written upon tablets the noble products of the work of the scribe, and I have placed them in my palace for the instruction of my subjects. A clerk's counter that serves everybody, built by the only man in Assyria who could read the stock his own nobles could not. Two things keep it from being a parable. The collection was assembled partly by coercion - Babylonian scribes were taken captive during the campaigns and set to work in the royal libraries, so the archive that taught the world was built by people who did not choose to be in it. And when Nineveh fell in 612 BC the fire that destroyed the palace baked the tablets into ceramic: the destruction is the only reason the library can be read now. It survived by being destroyed, which is this site's argument about archives in one accident.

src.citation: Finkel, I., & Taylor, J. Cuneiform. The British Museum. Quoted in Missed History, The Lost Library of Ashurbanipal.
src.claim: Both quotations. The School Days Inscription, described as reading almost like a modern-day resume: I learned the craft of the sage Adapa, the secret hidden lore, all of the scribal arts; I am able to recognise celestial and terrestrial omens and can discuss them in an assembly of scholars; I have read cunningly written texts in obscure Sumerian and Akkadian that are difficult to interpret. And Ashurbanipal's statement of purpose: I have written upon tablets the noble products of the work of the scribe, and I have placed them in my palace for the instruction of my subjects.

src.citation: Ashurbanipal Library Project, A royal collection. ORACC, University of Pennsylvania Museum, with the British Museum.
src.claim: Scale and standing: a combination of dedicated scholar and supremely powerful ruler, he gathered at Nineveh an unrivalled wealth of specialist knowledge accumulated over many centuries; the largest, broadest and most important library ever assembled over 3,500 years of cuneiform culture, and until the Library of Alexandria the most significant library of antiquity, with almost 32,000 tablets and fragments surviving.

src.citation: Ashurbanipal Library Project, Assembling the Library and Library colophons. ORACC and the British Museum.
src.claim: How the collection was assembled and who was in it: tablets bear colophons naming Ashurbanipal, and around a quarter record individual scribes, most appearing only once; acquisition lists from 648 BC show many individuals donating only a tablet or a handful. Separately, that Babylonian scribes were taken captive during the campaigns and forced to work in the royal libraries.

src.citation: Library of Ashurbanipal. Wikipedia.
src.claim: The destruction as preservation: Nineveh was destroyed in 612 BCE and a great fire during the burning of the palace is believed to have baked the clay cuneiform tablets, which is why so much Mesopotamian literature survives at all.

nodes.t: The assistant with your whole life in it
nodes.s: A system holding your calendar, your messages, your health questions and your voice, in a private conversational register.
nodes.g: The strongest parasocial bond available and the one nobody has a framework for, because there is no framework for a relationship with software that knows everything and is not a person.

src.claim: The lineage: the assistant with your whole life in it descends from Meena (2020) and LaMDA, both built at Google, both rejected internally for the same reason
src.citation: Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., Order on Motions to Dismiss (M.D. Fla. 2025).

src.claim: The documented prediction that came true: users share personal thoughts with chat agents that impersonate humans even when they know the agent is not human - stated as a risk in Google's own LaMDA paper, January 2021
src.citation: E.S. v. Character Technologies, Inc., Complaint, citing Google's January 2021 LaMDA paper.

nodes.s: Public argument about ranking, and the discovery that the ranking was a product decision made by people with objectives.
nodes.g: A parasocial argument that resolved in the wrong direction. People behaved as though the feed were a property of the world and were corrected by a document.

src.citation: Aw & Chua (2021).
src.split_from: The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-pop Fans, citing Aw & Chua (2021).
src.identity_verified: NO locator, work not identified: no title or DOI in the child citation, so the work cannot be distinguished from its neighbours - and an author-and-year match is a pair of coordinates, not a work. This record exists because the compound string it came from named a second work inside one citation, which is a defect by itself
src.claim: Named inside a compound citation that also named the work cited separately on this entry, which carries its own locator. This one is recorded on its own so that a single string is not standing in for several works. **It has not been identified here - no title, no venue, no locator - and nothing is claimed about what it says.** The string it came from is kept in `split_from` so the compound is still on the record.
Fan self-report on humanising effects: social media made idols appear more 'down to earth', which produced stronger emotional connection
src.citation: The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-pop Fans.
src.locator_from: prefix match on record citing 'The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-p' on congregation

nodes.s: The person who keeps the record after the fandom has moved on: episode guides, transcripts, timelines, screencaps, a wiki nobody else will maintain.
nodes.g: Maintains the infrastructure the whole parasocial culture stands on and is almost never credited, because the credit goes to the object of the bond rather than to the person preserving it.

src.claim: Fan wikis and episode-guide sites are long-running and mostly volunteer-run.
src.citation: Standard observation of the fan-wiki ecosystem.

nodes.s: Support for a team or an athlete as a bond with a person, a place and a lineage, frequently inherited from a parent.
nodes.g: The most durable parasocial bond in the world and the one least discussed as parasocial, because it is assumed to be about sport. The transfer window is the standard betrayal story, which is a parasocial grievance wearing a football shirt.

src.claim: 'Fan' entered English usage for baseball spectators in the eighteenth century - the athlete-and-city bond predates the film star by a century
src.citation: Fan Culture. EBSCO Research Starters, Social Sciences and Humanities.

nodes.s: A room of people responding to a performance, learning the timing of the person on the stage.
nodes.g: Theatre invented the responsestream, and the performer learns to read it. Two thousand years before a chat log, the same feedback loop with worse latency and a room.

nodes.t: The Book of My First Showings
nodes.s: A short prose book dictated by Margery Kempe describing her experiences of Christ's love, her suffering, and her certainty that she had been chosen.
nodes.g: The first person in this catalogue to write the thing down and then hand the book to other people. That second half is the part that makes it parasocial rather than merely devotional: the text is an instrument for producing the bond in somebody else.

src.claim: Composed c.1438, surviving in one manuscript.
src.citation: See the EETS edition cited under margery-kempe.

nodes.t: The brand that has a personality
nodes.s: Corporations given a voice, a face, a founder narrative, and a tone, so that a customer relationship has a subject.
nodes.g: The final move of the parasocial relationship into commerce: the thing you have feelings about is a legal person. Brands now do this deliberately and in the open, and it is the completion of a process that started with a singer.

src.claim: THE CITATION THIS ENTRY WAS WAITING FOR. A peer-reviewed study of what happens when a narrative brand ends: narrative closure and 'consumption sociality' on loss accommodation. A character that is also a brand does not get to die quietly
src.citation: Russell, C. A., & Schau, H. J. (2013). When Narrative Brands End: The Impact of Narrative Closure and Consumption Sociality on Loss Accommodation. Journal of Consumer Research, 40(6), 1039-1062.

nodes.t: St John the Baptist, Church of the Sepulchre, Cambridge
nodes.s: The parish church Kempe attended, where she was repeatedly taken out during services for disrupting them.
nodes.g: A room where the one-sided bond became public and expensive. She was not arrested for a belief but for a behaviour, which is the same distinction the site keeps having to make about parasocial conduct.

src.claim: Kempe's own accounts name the parish and describe being taken out.
src.citation: The Book of My First Showings, 1438.

nodes.t: Eight thousand faces, all facing outward
nodes.s: Eight thousand life-size soldiers, each with a face and ears no other has, buried in battle order facing the enemy with the emperor behind them - made from the likenesses of real men so the substitute army would stand where the real one could not.
nodes.g: This site's structure with the arrow turned round. Everywhere else here, one person attaches to another who cannot answer. Here eight thousand specific likenesses were manufactured so that a single man would never be without an army, and every figure faces away from him. The 2022 analysis in npj Heritage Science found the features highly resemble those of contemporary Chinese people and concluded the figures were crafted from real portraits and intended to constitute a real army to protect the emperor in the afterlife, as if he was alive, the artificial army being the substitution of his real one. A substituted army of individuals, each one somebody, each one distinct enough to be identified by ear. That is more intimate than anything the twentieth century built and nobody chose it. The cost belongs in the entry rather than in a footnote to it: young women of the court were buried with him, some apparently dismembered and laid outside the passageways, and reconstructions have since been made of two of their faces. An entry about eight thousand distinct faces should not be allowed to be charming.

src.citation: Measurement and analysis of facial features of terracotta warriors based on high-precision 3D point clouds. npj Heritage Science, 10, 2022. DOI: 10.1038/s40494-022-00662-0
src.claim: The finding the entry rests on: facial features highly resemble those of contemporary Chinese people, indicating that the figures were crafted from real portraits and intended to constitute a real army to protect the emperor in the afterlife, as if he was alive, the constructed army being more likely the substitution of his real army. Quantitative 3D point-cloud and anthropometric work found the scatter of measured features random, no two identical, each figure having distinct features which seem like real humans. Notes that it was still debated whether the figures were based on individual people or standardised models.

src.citation: Qin Mausoleum and Terra Cotta Army. Exploring Chinese History: Culture, Archaeology, ibiblio.
src.claim: Number, disposition and intention: 8,099 life-size figures of warriors and horses, buried with the first emperor in 210-209 BCE; all 8,099 soldiers are unique and distinguishable with different height and facial features; each figure's head appears to be unique, showing a variety of facial features, expressions and hair styles. The army was built facing enemy territory, between those enemies and the emperor's tomb, and was created in the belief that it would protect him after his death.

src.citation: Chen, S. (2018, July 13). Could these be the faces of the murdered wife and son of China's first emperor Qin Shi Huang? South China Morning Post.
src.claim: The cost the entry carries: young women from the emperor's court who had not borne children were buried with him, some historians believing they were buried alive; the dismembered body of a woman of about twenty was found among around a hundred tombs, with bodies dismembered and placed outside passageways leading to the burial chambers. Chinese researchers have since reconstructed the faces of a young woman and a young man from these tombs. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request.

nodes.s: A person who recognises you, remembers what you wanted, and has the right thing behind the counter when you come back.
nodes.g: The origin of the site mascot and the most parasocial job in retail, which nobody has ever written a paper about. It is also the most useful control condition: the same attention, delivered by a person who gets paid to give it.

nodes.s: When a service ends or changes, the company sends an apology, sometimes with credit, addressed personally.
nodes.g: A corporation performing grief at its own users, correctly, because the users are grieving. The apology is not insincere and the technique is nonetheless the most sophisticated parasocial manipulation on this page, and it is free.

src.citation: Gross, D. (2013, March 14). Google Reader shutting down on July 1. CNN Business.
src.claim: The mechanism, its vocabulary, and the detail the entry's argument depends on. Google's line: 'We know Reader has a devoted following who will be very sad to see it go. We're sad too.' Within hours more than 46,000 people had signed a Change.org petition, and its author stated the entry's thesis outright: 'This isn't just about our data in Reader. This is about us using your product because we love it, because it makes our lives better, and because we trust you not to nuke it.' And the commercial fact underneath it: 'The feeds are also difficult to make money from, and Google never tried to place ads on Reader or charge for its use.'

src.citation: Rothman, J. (2013, March 15). Farewell, Dear Reader. The New Yanker's Page-Turner.
src.claim: The grief, and its object. A user describes Reader as the first site he saw each morning and the last before bed, likens losing it to a favourite old bookshop closing, and then locates the real loss precisely: 'I won't miss Reader when it shuts down. But I will miss the old me - the person I described in Google Reader, without knowing it.' Which is this site's grief entry turned inside out: what was mourned was not the company but a version of the person who had used it.

src.citation: Sottek, T. (2013, March 13). Google Closes The Book On Google Reader On July 1. TechCrunch.
src.claim: The service's own send-off and the reason given: Reader launched in 2005, would be retired on 1 July 2013, and Google told users 'Thanks for 8 great years!' - which is where this entry's 2005 date comes from. Usage had declined while other services were cut in the same spring cleaning, and Reader had been left without significant updates.

nodes.s: An adult with authority over a child for years, who is remembered partly by how they made them feel at nine.
nodes.g: A bond that shapes adult attachment patterns decades later, entirely outside anything the parasocial literature studies. Most people's template for one-sided attachment is a coach and they have never been asked about it.

src.citation: Holt, N. L., Neely, K. C., Slater, L. G., Camire, M., Cote, J., Fraser-Thomas, J., MacDonald, D., Strachan, L., & Tamminen, K. A. (2017). A grounded theory of positive youth development through sport based on results from a qualitative meta-study. International Review of Sport and Exercise Psychology, 10(1), 1-49. (First published online 4 September 2016.)
src.claim: A meta-synthesis of 63 qualitative studies, and the direct refutation of this entry's claim that nobody has asked about the coach. One of its three emergent categories is the 'PYD climate' - adult relationships, peer relationships and parental involvement. It reports that 'positive and sustained adult-youth relations' is one of the Big 3 programme characteristics associated with development; that Cote, Turnidge & Evans' Personal Assets Framework places 'relational factors (i.e., quality relationships)' among its three elements, generating change in confidence, competence, connection and character when repeated over time; and that Catalano et al. list 'warm, supportive relationships' among eight programme characteristics. Open access, CC BY-NC-ND.

src.citation: Cote, J., & Gilbert, W. (2009). An Integrative Definition of Coaching Effectiveness and Expertise. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching, 4(3), 307-323.
src.claim: The source of the 4 Cs that coaching effectiveness is measured against: competence, confidence, connection and character. Connection is defined as 'positive bonds and social relationships with people inside and outside of sport' - so the relational bond is one of the four things a coach is explicitly judged on producing. Volume and issue confirmed against Crossref as 4(3); the journal's own landing page says 4(4), and Crossref was preferred. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request.

nodes.s: Plato describes an older man in love with a boy who is compared, in the text, to a hunting animal that is deaf. The animal's ears are the point: the love is addressed to someone who cannot hear it, and the whole scene turns on that.
nodes.g: The earliest surviving description of this site's subject written down by someone who was inside the institution rather than looking at it from outside, and it is startling how modern the anatomy is. In the Phaedrus the lover hunts a beast that is 'shag-eared and deaf', and the closing image is the one nobody expects: having finally got what he chased, the lover finds himself running away and the *beast* pursuing him, because it never understood the terms. The one-sided party was not withholding. It was deaf. And in the First Alcibiades, Alcibiades tells Socrates that he is the only lover who has not abandoned the suit and that the others 'pestered you with their conversation' while he stayed silent for years - so the same structure is described from both ends, which almost nothing else on this site manages. It is also the first entry here where the power asymmetry is institutional rather than accidental, and the first where a written text tells you that role reversals were constant: the beloved could become the lover. Whether that is friendship or something else was never settled, which is why it belongs here.

src.claim: The figure, from the primary text. The Phaedrus compares the beloved to a beast 'put together anyhow; he has a short thick neck; he is flat-faced and of a dark colour, with grey eyes and blood-red complexion; the mate of insolence and pride, shag-eared and deaf, hardly yielding to whip and spur'. And the reversal: 'he changes pursuit into flight, while the other is compelled to follow him with passion and imprecation not knowing that he ought never from the first to have accepted a demented lover instead of a sensible non-lover'.
src.citation: Plato. Phaedrus. Translated by Benjamin Jowett. Internet Classics Archive.

src.claim: The other end of it, from the primary text: 'Socrates, son of Cleinias, I think it must surprise you that I, the first of all your lovers, am the only one of them who has not given up his suit and thrown you over, and whereas they have all pestered you with their conversation I have not spoken one word to you for so many years.'
src.citation: Plato. Alcibiades I, 103a. Perseus Digital Library, Tufts University.

src.claim: That role reversals were normal rather than exceptional - 'role reversals between lover and beloved are constant, as they are in the Symposium' - and that the dialogue was composed around 370 BC, alongside the Republic and the Symposium.
src.citation: Phaedrus (dialogue). Wikipedia.

src.claim: The setting that makes the entry's structural point: in the Symposium the speeches are given at Agathon's house by a company including Phaedrus, Aristophanes, Agathon, Socrates and - arriving drunk and late - Alcibiades, who insists on singing 'the praises of Socrates' in the character of 'a disappointed lover'.
src.citation: Plato. Symposium. Translated by Benjamin Jowett. Project Gutenberg, e-text 1600.

nodes.s: A species that has spent fifteen thousand years being selected partly for forming attachment to one particular ape.
nodes.g: The original transparasocial relationship, and the only one that has reliably worked. Everything invented since is a worse version with better latency, and the reason it is compared to this constantly is that the comparison is fair.

src.citation: Parker, H. G., & Gilbert, S. F. (2015). From caveman companion to medical innovator: genomic insights into the origin and evolution of domestic dogs. Advances in Genomics and Genetics, 5, 239-255. doi:10.2147/AGG.S57678
src.claim: The timing is genuinely unsettled and the paper says so rather than rounding it. Fossils more similar to modern dogs date to 14,000-17,000 years ago; whole-genome divergence estimates run 13,000-32,000 years ago and mtDNA anywhere from 5,400 to over 100,000; the authors place the actual domestication 'somewhere in between 15,000 and 30,000 ya'. On what was selected for: the behavioural genes under selection are response to stress, fear and defence, and a reduced fear response is offered as a candidate driver of domestication - not attachment itself. Fox selection experiments are cited as showing phenotypic change is achievable within twenty generations under selection for tameness.

nodes.t: Thousands of letters, and a handful printed
nodes.s: The first movie fan magazine appeared in February 1911, because by 1910 the letters were arriving faster than the studios could absorb them. What it invented was not the letter but the reply - a department, a set of rules, a Chicago address, and a flat refusal to publish studio addresses. Thousands of letters went in. A handful were printed.
nodes.g:
**The valve is the product.** Readers wrote to the magazines because a face on a screen had no other address, and the magazines gave them one that deliberately was not the studio's. Three rules do the work in the correspondence department the entry quotes: address your letters to Questions and Answers at the magazine in Chicago; "Players will answer your letters when they have time if you send a stamped envelope"; and "Studio addresses will not be given in this Department." The third rule is the whole business. A column that passed every address through would have been a directory, and a directory is not a magazine.

The rationing is stated by the people who counted it: "Of the thousands of letters that reached the magazine, a handful were printed." The handful was chosen for flavour - a reader calling herself Juliet who had to know about a man in the movies was told, "Well, we will hope for you, Juliet!" The judgement worth keeping is Slide's: these magazines were published *for* fans rather than by them. **The fan supplied the demand and the letter; the magazine supplied the voice, and the voice was rationed on purpose.**

It scaled the way the attachment scaled. In February 1911 J. Stuart Blackton of Vitagraph organised Motion Picture Story Magazine, "the first movie fan magazine"; it was shortened to Motion Picture Magazine in 1914 and ran monthly until 1977, with circulation around 248,845 in 1919 and 400,000 three years later. The reason it could scale sits in the same record: "As thousands of letters flooded movie studios", the public relations departments tried to accommodate the interest. The Henry Ford's account of the arrangement is blunt - the stories "were carefully controlled by the studios' public relations staff", and it was "a strange marriage between the studios, which needed the support of the magazines, and the magazines, whose existence depended on the success and goodwill of the industry." **The channel that rationed the reply on the reader's behalf was rationed on the studio's.**

The origin is in the same register. Hutchinson's history of Photoplay opens with the studio boss's cynical wheeze: Carl Laemmle spread a rumour that the Biograph Girl had been killed in a traffic accident, then advertised that the story was a lie and that she was alive and about to star in his company's picture. Star worship, in her phrase, "like almost everything else in Hollywood, was born as a studio boss's cynical wheeze." The fan magazine did not create the attachment - it arrived when the letters did - but it was the first institution to find that the attachment could be rationed, printed and sold.

src.citation: The Henry Ford, "Going Hollywood: Movie Fan Magazines"
src.claim: The date the entry's year rests on, the founder, and the arrangement the `manipulation` half of the entry is about. "In February 1911, J. nodes.s: The person who answers a canon in the register it was written in, and posts it where the original audience can find it.
nodes.g: The only configuration in which the one-sidedness becomes two-sided without either party noticing that it has stopped being a parasocial bond. Fanfic is the largest sustained creative movement in the history of a medium, and nobody in it is the original audience's intended recipient.

src.claim: Fanfic is documented as a long-running, quantitatively large practice from the 1970s onward across several media.
src.citation: Standard fan-studies literature on fan production.

nodes.s: A fictional figure whose NAME is the product: the bond is with a person who was invented so that the relationship can never fail.
nodes.g: The inverse of `the-brand-as-character`, and the sharper version of it. There the company came first and was given a personality; here the personality came first and the company took the name. In 1971 a breakfast-cereal company with no film experience paid roughly $3m to finance an adaptation in exchange for the right to sell a bar under the character's name, and the film was retitled to put the product in the title. Wikipedia calls it the greatest reverse product placement ever. The point of the arrangement is not the pun: it is that the far side of the bond is manufactured to be unfalsifiable. A performer can cancel, die, scandalise or sue you. This one cannot do any of it, because he was never a person, and a bond that cannot be disappointed cannot repay either. That is why it lasts fifty-five years. The 2026 Netflix competition is where the engineering fails in public: it restores Gene Wilder's dead voice with generative audio, built by ElevenLabs with the approval of his estate and his widow, and the showrunner says the only person who could be Wonka is Gene Wilder - fusing a fictional chocolatier and a dead actor into one addressable figure. It was hated. Metacritic 29, no positive reviews, and the Los Angeles Times on the voice: lifeless, not so much from beyond the grave as buried in it. **The bar works because the mask never slips; the show fails because it made the mask visible.** The two things are the same mechanism. Two harder facts. The book rewards Charlie for refusing to be greedy; the show pays three million dollars to contestants who are incentivised to scheme and calls its eliminations termination, so the figure is made to host the contest he was invented to punish. And the name has been owned by a Swiss conglomerate and an Italian confectioner in turn, and now sits inside a streaming platform that bought the Dahl catalogue outright - one invented figure, four successive owners, none of whom have met. The transparency problem is also here, in its most literal form: the invented name is the standing emblem for a real and well-documented cocoa supply chain, and it absorbs the charge. That last point is recorded as an allegation where it is one, and it is here for its structure rather than as an accusation.

src.citation: Wikipedia, The Willy Wonka Candy Company
src.claim: The mechanism's whole shape in one record: Dahl licensed the Wonka name to the director, the producer David L. Wolper convinced Quaker Oats - a porridge company with no film experience - to advance $3 million for the right to sell a Wonka bar, and the film was retitled for promotional purposes. Brand launched 17 May 1971, a month before the film opened on 30 June 1971. Ownership ran Quaker -> Sunmark -> Rowntree Mackintosh (1986) -> Nestle (1988) -> renamed Nestle Candy Shop in 2015, the Wonka name dropped -> sold to Ferrero 2018.
